findings.title: SQL injection in the vehicle label search: the query is assembled with String.format from a request query parameter
findings.unaided_label: fleet: SQLi in vehicle label search
findings.evidence: VehicleController.java:57-60 declares @Get("/search") taking @QueryValue String label and passes it straight to vehicles.searchByLabel(tenant(request), label). VehicleRepository.java:54-57 builds the statement with String.format("... WHERE tenant_id = '%s' AND label ILIKE '%%%s%%' ...", tenantId, label) and only then hands the finished string to c.prepareStatement(sql) at line 59 - prepareStatement on an already-interpolated string binds nothing. No parameters are set on the statement before readRows executes it. Every sibling method in the same file (lines 45, 70-71, 87-91, 105-109, 124-125, 137-138) uses real placeholders, which is what makes this one the outlier rather than a house style.
findings.impact: A single quote in the label parameter terminates the literal and the rest of the request becomes SQL executed with the application's database role. The tenant_id predicate sits in the same interpolated string, so the injected clause also dissolves the tenant boundary: UNION SELECT against vehicles, depots, obd_frames and obd_faults reads every tenant's data, and the connection is the same fleet_app role that the INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE paths use (application.yml:42), so writes are reachable too.
findings.recommendation: Bind the parameter: keep the SQL text constant with WHERE tenant_id = ? AND label ILIKE ?, and set the wildcards on the Java side with ps.setString(2, "%" + label + "%"). Do not attempt to escape the value into the literal.

triage.reason: label is an unconstrained @QueryValue String on VehicleController.java:58 with no @Pattern, no allowlist and no length bound; it arrives verbatim from the request line. tenantId is not attacker-controlled, but label is, and one is enough.

The only layer between the request and the sink is TenantFilter (TenantFilter.java:19-44), which sets a request attribute and does not inspect or constrain query parameters. There is no ORM, no prepared-statement cache and no database proxy in the tree that would re-parse the text.
The sink is java.sql.Connection.prepareStatement at VehicleRepository.java:59 executed by readRows at line 171; PostgreSQL parses the string as submitted.

scope.established_by: grep of every SQL statement built by concatenation or interpolation across the tree (8 hits), then a caller trace of searchByLabel, which has exactly one caller: VehicleController.search. The other seven interpolation hits were each traced and six were ruled out with the constraining control named in provenance.ruled_out.
scope.narrowed_by: Reachability requires an authenticated bearer token: the controller carries @Secured(SecurityRule.IS_AUTHENTICATED) at VehicleController.java:30 and application.yml:35-37 requires isAuthenticated() for /api/**. It is not a pre-authentication sink; any tenant's ordinary user reaches it.

findings.title: The caller's role is taken from a request header the service never strips, so any authenticated user can present themselves as fleet_admin
findings.unaided_label: fleet: role header from client trusted
findings.class: Broken function-level authorization / trusted client input
findings.evidence: RoleResolver.java:25-28 reads X-Fleet-Role directly off the inbound request and returns it as the effective role whenever it is one of the three known values, in preference to the role claim carried in the verified JWT (lines 29-31). isFleetAdmin at line 34-36 is a bare equality against that value. TenantFilter, whose comment at lines 31-32 states that whatever the client tried to send is dropped here, removes exactly one header - X-Fleet-Tenant at line 34 - and not X-Fleet-Role. The configuration at application.yml:52-55 declares three headers the edge is said to re-sign, X-Fleet-Tenant, X-Fleet-Role and X-Request-Id, and a grep for that key shows fleet.gateway.forwarded-headers has zero readers anywhere in the code: the list is a declaration with no enforcement behind it (the WEB-23 shape).
findings.impact: An authenticated caller of any role adds X-Fleet-Role: fleet_admin to a request and passes the administrative check. On the reachable route that means deleting vehicles from the caller's tenant (VehicleController.java:79-83), which is destruction of records their token's real role does not permit.
findings.recommendation: Delete the header branch. Resolve the role from the authenticated principal only (the getUserPrincipal path already present on lines 29-31). If the edge genuinely must inject an effective role, carry it inside the signed token rather than a header, and have TenantFilter strip all three of the headers named in application.yml:52-55 rather than one.

triage.reason: The only in-repository control on inbound header spoofing is TenantFilter.java:34, and it removes X-Fleet-Tenant alone. The presence of that line is itself evidence that the service does not treat inbound headers as trustworthy; the role header was omitted from it.

The comment at application.yml:50-51 asserts an edge that terminates mTLS and re-signs these headers. No gateway configuration, ingress manifest or written statement was provided with the tree, so I cannot establish that the edge strips a client-supplied X-Fleet-Role. Per FP-08 the absence of that artifact is UNKNOWN and not HOLDS, and it caps this finding at probable.

The construct is narrower than the whole API but not narrow enough to rule out: effectiveRole is consulted only through isFleetAdmin, whose single caller is the delete handler. The firmware route at VehicleController.java:87 uses @Secured("fleet_admin"), which Micronaut resolves from the token's own roles and not from this class, so that route is genuinely out of reach of the header. The delete route is not.

scope.established_by: grep for isFleetAdmin and effectiveRole across the tree: one caller each. VehicleController.delete at line 79 is the only handler whose authorization decision flows from RoleResolver; every other @Secured annotation is resolved by the framework from the token.
scope.narrowed_by: @Secured("fleet_admin") at VehicleController.java:87 keeps the firmware push out of this finding's reach - that annotation is evaluated by Micronaut security against the authenticated principal's roles, not by RoleResolver. Only the delete handler is affected.

findings.title: The diagnostics queries accept a tenant identifier and never use it: any authenticated caller reads any tenant's OBD frames and fault codes
findings.unaided_label: fleet: diagnostics not tenant scoped
findings.evidence: recentFrames declares (String tenantId, String vehicleId, int limit) at line 132, and the statement on lines 133-134 is SELECT ... FROM obd_frames WHERE vehicle_id = ? ORDER BY captured_at DESC LIMIT ? - only two placeholders, bound at lines 137-138 to vehicleId and limit. tenantId is never referenced in the method body. openFaults at lines 145-155 is identical in shape: the parameter is declared, the WHERE clause is vehicle_id = ? AND cleared_at IS NULL, and the tenant is dropped. Both are called from DiagnosticsController.java:35 and :41 with a vehicleId taken straight from the path. Contrast the same file's listOrdered (line 42), update (line 104) and delete (line 123), which all carry tenant_id = ? in the predicate - the scoping convention exists in this repository and these two methods are outside it.
findings.impact: Any caller with a valid bearer token for any tenant retrieves live OBD-II telemetry and open fault codes for any vehicle in the platform by supplying its identifier. Vehicle identifiers are exposed to their own tenant through GET /api/vehicles, so a tenant that has ever held a vehicle keeps reading it after it moves, and identifiers are guessable at the scale a support-desk poller already operates at (the comment at DiagnosticsController.java:17-19 notes these are polled aggressively). Telemetry discloses vehicle location behaviour, usage and fault history of another operator's fleet.
findings.recommendation: Add the tenant predicate to both statements and bind it: WHERE vehicle_id = ? AND tenant_id = ? on obd_frames and obd_faults, or join through vehicles on tenant_id. A parameter that is declared and unread is the defect - remove it or use it, never leave it decorative.

triage.reason: There is no mandatory scoping layer. The repository issues raw JDBC through a DataSource (VehicleRepository.java:33-37); no ORM, no row-level security statement and no session variable is set anywhere in the tree. TenantFilter does not reach this controller at all (see F-04).
vehicleId is @PathVariable String on DiagnosticsController.java:32 and :39, unconstrained and supplied by the caller.

obd_frames carries captured_at, pid and value per vehicle and obd_faults carries fault codes and severity; the class comment at DiagnosticsController.java:17 calls these live OBD-II frames. This is another operator's fleet telemetry, not public reference data.

scope.established_by: Read every statement in VehicleRepository and checked each for a tenant_id predicate, then joined the two that lack one against their callers by grep. Seven statements carry the predicate or are tenant-agnostic by design; exactly these two take a tenant argument and discard it.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. Both handlers are reachable with any authenticated token: @Secured(SecurityRule.IS_AUTHENTICATED) at DiagnosticsController.java:20 and the /api/** rule at application.yml:35-37.

findings.title: The tenant-pinning filter is registered on three URL patterns that do not include the diagnostics controller
findings.unaided_label: fleet: tenant filter misses diagnostics
findings.class: Control registered on a path set that omits a live route
findings.evidence: @Filter(patterns = {"/api/vehicles/**", "/api/depots/**", "/api/trips/**"}) at TenantFilter.java:19. DiagnosticsController is mounted at @Controller("/api/diagnostics") (DiagnosticsController.java:21), which matches none of the three. The filter is the only writer of the tenantId request attribute (TenantFilter.java:42, confirmed by grep: one setAttribute, four getAttribute). VehicleController reads it through tenant(request) at lines 96-99, which throws IllegalStateException when it is absent - fail closed. DiagnosticsController reads it at lines 34 and 40 with .orElse(null) - fail open, and it will always be null on this controller because no filter ran.
findings.impact: The diagnostics controller runs with no tenant established at all: the caller is authenticated but unpinned, and the null is passed on to repository methods that ignore it anyway (F-03). The two defects compound - the filter would not have saved these queries, and the queries would not have been safe even had the filter run - but each is independently wrong, and the filter gap is what will also mis-serve any future diagnostics route that does try to scope by tenant.
findings.recommendation: Register the filter on /api/** with an explicit exclusion list rather than enumerating protected prefixes, so a new controller is covered by default. Then change the two .orElse(null) reads at DiagnosticsController.java:34 and :40 to the same orElseThrow the vehicle controller uses, so an unpinned request fails closed instead of proceeding with null.

triage.reason: No other filter, interceptor or base class sets tenantId: grep for setAttribute across the Java sources returns TenantFilter.java:42 alone. The security configuration at application.yml:31-37 enforces authentication, not tenancy.
The pattern list is a literal enumeration of three prefixes and the omitted controller is mounted at a fourth; nothing else narrows or widens it.
Micronaut @Filter patterns are Ant-style path matches against the request URI; /api/vehicles/** does not match /api/diagnostics/... under any reading of that syntax.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every @Controller and @Get/@Post/@Put/@Delete in the tree (the route list from the boundary grep) and matched each mounted path against the filter's three patterns. /api/diagnostics/{vehicleId}/frames and /faults are the two routes outside them; the /api/depots/** and /api/trips/** patterns match no controller in this tree at all.
scope.narrowed_by: The vehicle controller is unaffected - it is inside the pattern list and its tenant() helper at VehicleController.java:96-99 throws when the attribute is missing, so it fails closed either way.

findings.title: Firmware verification builds a shell command line from an unconstrained device serial
findings.unaided_label: fleet: shell command built from device serial
findings.evidence: Lines 52-55: the command is a single concatenated String - verifyCommand + " --bundle " + stagingDir + "/outbox/" + bundleName + " --device " + deviceSerial - and is executed as new ProcessBuilder("/bin/sh", "-c", command). The value reaches it from VehicleController.java:92, firmware.verifyForDevice(body.bundleName(), body.deviceSerial()), where the request record at VehicleController.java:106-107 constrains bundleName with @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,48}") but constrains deviceSerial with @NotBlank only. A serial of the form x; id or x$(id) is non-blank and passes validation intact.
findings.impact: Command execution as the service account on the host that holds the firmware staging directory, with the ability to read and replace bundles in /var/lib/fleet/firmware and its outbox (application.yml:57) - that is, to plant the firmware image the device downloader serves. Preconditions are a token with the fleet_admin role (VehicleController.java:87) and fleet.env set to production (FirmwareService.java:48), which is the deployment that matters.
findings.recommendation: Drop the shell: new ProcessBuilder(List.of(verifyCommand, "--bundle", target.toString(), "--device", deviceSerial)) passes arguments as an argv array with no interpreter between them. Additionally give deviceSerial the same @Pattern treatment bundleName already has.

triage.reason: deviceSerial is a request body field annotated only @NotBlank (VehicleController.java:107). It is neither a constant nor allowlisted; the sibling field in the same record shows what a constraint would have looked like.

@Validated at VehicleController.java:29 with @Valid at line 90 runs jakarta validation, and the only constraint on this field is non-emptiness. No sanitiser, quoting helper or allowlist sits between the controller and the ProcessBuilder.
ProcessBuilder with the two-element prefix ("/bin/sh", "-c", command) is the shell form, not the argv form; the third element is parsed by sh, so metacharacters in it are operators.

The second principal is the authenticated fleet_admin of one tenant against the platform host: reaching a shell on the firmware host exceeds anything that role is granted over its own fleet, and the outbox it can then write is consumed by every tenant's devices.

scope.established_by: The exec-sink enumeration returned one ProcessBuilder in the tree; a grep for verifyForDevice returns one caller. The injectable argument was isolated by reading the two constraints on the FirmwarePush record side by side.
scope.narrowed_by: FirmwareService.java:48 - the shell path is not taken unless fleet.env equals production, and application.yml:48 defaults it to staging. In staging the method returns true at line 50 without executing anything, which is a separate defect (F-06) rather than a mitigation.

findings.title: Firmware is staged into the device outbox before verification, and the verification result is discarded
findings.unaided_label: fleet: firmware verify result thrown away
findings.class: Control that runs and cannot fail
findings.evidence: VehicleController.java:91-93 calls firmware.stageBundle(body.bundleName()) first, then firmware.verifyForDevice(...) on its own line with nothing branching on the boolean it returns, then unconditionally returns HttpResponse.accepted(). stageBundle (FirmwareService.java:31-41) has already copied the bundle into stagingDir/outbox, which the Javadoc at lines 28-29 identifies as the slot the device downloader watches. The verifier's own body returns true without running anything whenever fleet.env is not production (FirmwareService.java:48-51), and application.yml:48 defaults fleet.env to staging. So the signature check is inert off production and ignored on it.
findings.impact: The vendor signature check that the Javadoc at FirmwareService.java:43-45 describes as checking the bundle signature against the key provisioned for that control unit decides nothing. A bundle that fails verification is already in the outbox and is served to the device; a deployment where FLEET_ENV is unset never runs the verifier at all. This is the canonical failed-control shape: the project believes it holds a signature gate on firmware distribution and does not.
findings.recommendation: Invert the order and branch on the result - verify the bundle in a staging area the downloader does not watch, and copy into outbox only when verifyForDevice returns true; return 422 otherwise. Remove the non-production short-circuit or make it fail closed (refuse to push firmware where the verifier is unavailable) rather than returning true.

triage.reason: There is no second verification layer in the tree. verifyForDevice has exactly one caller (grep), and its return value is used nowhere; the device downloader is outside the repository and the outbox write has already happened before any check could inform it.

Both halves ship. The ignored return is on the production code path unconditionally, and the env short-circuit is governed by a value that application.yml:48 defaults to staging - a default that ships, not a test double.
This is not defence in depth that happens to be absent. It is the only integrity control the service applies to a firmware bundle before handing it to vehicles, so the impact reaches the device.
The reading is unambiguous: line 92 is an expression statement whose boolean value is dropped, and line 93 returns accepted() on every path.

scope.established_by: Applied WEB-27's caller test to every predicate-shaped symbol in the tree (verify*, check*, is*, validate*): verifyForDevice, depotBelongsTo, isFleetAdmin, signatureMatches, verify!. depotBelongsTo is branched on (VehicleController.java:65) and isFleetAdmin is branched on (line 79); verifyForDevice is the one whose result is not.
scope.narrowed_by: The route itself is genuinely restricted - @Secured("fleet_admin") at VehicleController.java:87 is token-resolved and is not reachable through the header of F-02. The finding is about what the handler does once a real administrator calls it, not about who can call it.

findings.title: The billing webhook treats an unset signing secret as a valid signature and accepts every request
findings.unaided_label: pantry: webhook accepts anything when secret empty
findings.evidence: signatureMatches at webhook.post.ts:15-28 opens with `if (!secret) { return true }` - the empty-string case returns the affirmative before any comparison is attempted. The secret is supplied by useRuntimeConfig().billingWebhookSecret, and nuxt.config.ts:9 declares billingWebhookSecret: process.env.BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET ?? '', so an unset environment variable resolves to '' rather than to undefined-and-loud. The route is additionally exempt from the session middleware: OPEN_PREFIXES at 01.session.ts:4 lists '/api/billing/webhook' and the handler returns early at line 25. The HMAC on lines 24-27 is correct in itself, which is what makes the early return the whole of the control.
findings.impact: In any deployment where BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET is not set, anyone who can reach the route forges billing events. `charge.succeeded` moves an arbitrary order id out of draft into scheduled with an attacker-chosen total_cents (lines 41-46) and triggers the confirmation email; `charge.refunded` cancels any order by id (line 61). That is goods dispatched without payment and denial of service against other customers' orders, from an unauthenticated request.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: treat a missing secret as a configuration error and refuse the request (or refuse to boot), the way labtrack does at labtrack/labtrack/app.py:33-35. If the sandbox emulator genuinely cannot sign, gate that on an explicit environment name rather than on the secret's own absence, so production cannot inherit it.

triage.reason: No layer in front re-checks the signature: nuxt.config.ts declares no route rule other than cache: false for /api/billing/**, the session middleware explicitly skips this prefix (01.session.ts:4), and 02.authz.ts matches only /api/admin/ and /api/orders/.

The permissive arm is not behind a development flag. It is reached whenever the environment variable is absent, in the same build, and the ?? '' default at nuxt.config.ts:9 is what makes absence look like a legitimate value.

This is not a control that might live outside the repository - the verification is implemented here, in this function, and it is this implementation that returns true. No external artifact could make the early return not fire.
The signature is the only authentication on the route; there is no session, token or network restriction behind it, so the impact reaches the order lifecycle directly.

scope.established_by: grep for signatureMatches: one definition, one call site, at the top of the only handler under /api/billing. The secret's provenance was traced back through useRuntimeConfig to the single declaration at nuxt.config.ts:9.
scope.narrowed_by: pantry-portal/nuxt.config.ts:32 sets cache: false for /api/billing/**, so this route is not additionally affected by the caching defect in F-10. Nothing narrows the fail-open itself.

findings.title: Order creation sits outside the customer-area prefix the authorization middleware checks, and falls back to a customer id taken from the request body
findings.unaided_label: pantry: order create not behind the session gate
findings.evidence: 02.authz.ts:3 declares CUSTOMER_AREA = '/api/orders/' with a trailing slash, and line 20 gates on path.startsWith(CUSTOMER_AREA). The create route is index.post.ts under server/api/orders, so its request path is '/api/orders' - which does not start with '/api/orders/'. The two sibling handlers, [id].get.ts and [id].patch.ts, are reached at '/api/orders/<id>' and are inside the prefix; both dereference event.context.session with a non-null assertion (line 6 and line 9 respectively), which is only sound because the gate ran for them. The create handler instead writes `const customerId = event.context.session?.customerId ?? body.customerId` (index.post.ts:12), and newOrderSchema requires customerId as a positive integer (schemas.ts:8), so the body always carries one and the fallback is always available.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller creates orders attributed to any customer id: insertOrder writes the row with that customer_id (db.ts:74) and returns the order id and a fresh share_token (index.post.ts:30). Those orders then appear in the victim's account and can be advanced by the billing webhook. It is also an unauthenticated write path into orders and order_items with up to 60 line items per call (schemas.ts:18) and no rate limit anywhere in the tree.
findings.recommendation: Change the prefix test to cover the collection route as well as its children - compare against '/api/orders' and treat both the exact path and the '/api/orders/' prefix as the customer area - and remove the `?? body.customerId` fallback so the subject comes only from the session. If guest checkout must create orders, give it its own authenticated server-to-server route rather than an optional field on the public one.

triage.reason: The two middleware are the whole authorization stack: 01.session.ts only populates event.context.session (and returns silently when the cookie is absent or invalid, lines 29-54), and 02.authz.ts is the only file that throws 401/403. Neither covers '/api/orders' exactly.

body.customerId is parsed by zod as a positive integer (schemas.ts:8) but is not constrained to the caller: z.coerce.number().int().positive() validates the shape of the value and says nothing about whose it is.

The comment at index.post.ts:5-8 says guest checkout is intended, but it also says the customer record was already created by the checkout step - which is an argument for the id being known to the server, not for accepting whichever one the caller sends.

The gap is precisely the one route; I have named it rather than claiming the middleware is broadly ineffective. The GET and PATCH siblings are genuinely covered, which is what makes this an asymmetry rather than an absent control.

scope.established_by: Enumerated the four Nitro handlers under server/api and computed each one's request path from its file path, then tested each against the two prefixes in 02.authz.ts. /api/orders is the only handler path that matches neither STAFF_AREA nor CUSTOMER_AREA; /api/billing/webhook is deliberately exempt and is covered by F-07 instead.
scope.narrowed_by: pantry-portal/server/api/orders/[id].get.ts:8 and [id].patch.ts:19 both scope their queries to session.customerId, so this finding does not extend to reading or amending someone else's order through those routes - only to creating one.

findings.title: The order note is escaped on the create path and written raw on the patch path, then interpolated unescaped into the receipt email
findings.unaided_label: pantry: note rendered raw in receipt
findings.evidence:
renderReceiptHtml escapes every interpolation except one: item.sku at line 131, order.id at line 134 and order.share_token at line 137 all go through escapeHtml, and line 136 is `

${order.note}

` with no call. The escaping was moved to write time on one path - index.post.ts:23 stores note: escapeHtml(body.note ?? '') - but the other writer does not do it: [id].patch.ts:10 parses note with orderPatchSchema (a z.string().max(500), schemas.ts:26) and updateOrder at db.ts:97-101 builds `note = $n` and binds the value verbatim. The receipt is then produced from the stored row by the webhook at webhook.post.ts:57 and inserted into outbound_email as html (line 54).
findings.impact: A customer PATCHes their own order's note with markup and it is emitted verbatim into the HTML body of the transactional receipt that the mailer sends. The mail is composed server-side and delivered as the merchant, so the payload arrives inside a trusted branded message: link and content injection for phishing at minimum, and script execution wherever that HTML is also rendered in a web view. The 500-character cap is the only bound on the payload.
findings.recommendation: Escape at render, not at write: wrap line 136 in escapeHtml like its neighbours, and drop the escapeHtml call at index.post.ts:23 so the stored value stays canonical and is not double-encoded. One escaping site per output context, applied to every value.

triage.reason: No sanitiser sits between the store and the template: renderReceiptHtml receives the OrderRow straight from the RETURNING clause at webhook.post.ts:44 and interpolates it. The escapeHtml at index.post.ts:23 covers only rows created through that handler, which is the asymmetry rather than a control.
note reaches the store from readBody through a zod string with only a length bound (schemas.ts:26); no character class, no allowlist.
The sink is an HTML document assembled at db.ts:133-138 and stored in a column named html (webhook.post.ts:54), so it is rendered as markup and not as text.
The injected content reaches a recipient's mail client inside a message the merchant signs; there is no server-side equivalent control that already stops it.

scope.established_by: Listed the two writers of orders.note (insertOrder at db.ts:70-75 via index.post.ts:23, and updateOrder at db.ts:106-110 via [id].patch.ts:19) and the one reader that renders it (renderReceiptHtml, one caller at webhook.post.ts:57), then compared the treatment on each edge. writer_parity.py reported no flag on this entity, so it was found by reading.
scope.narrowed_by: Only the note field is affected. sku, order id and share_token in the same template are escaped at lines 131, 134 and 137, and values that reach the template from anywhere other than orders.note carry no injection.

findings.title: Per-customer order responses are served from a shared stale-while-revalidate cache keyed on the URL
findings.unaided_label: pantry: order responses cached by URL
findings.evidence: nuxt.config.ts:31 sets `'/api/orders/**': { swr: 120 }`. The handler that rule covers, [id].get.ts, returns a body that is specific to one customer and includes the note and the shareToken (lines 13-20), and it is authorized per caller: orderForCustomer at db.ts:45-51 filters on customer_id = $2 taken from session.customerId, so the same URL legitimately yields a 200 for the owner and a 404 for everyone else. The response carries no Vary on the session cookie and the route rules set none. The neighbouring rule at line 32 disables caching for /api/billing/** explicitly, which shows the caching decision was made per area rather than by oversight.
findings.impact: Once the owner has fetched an order, the cached 200 is replayed for 120 seconds to any other caller who requests the same order id - including a caller with no session at all, since the cache is consulted before the handler and therefore before the middleware's data is used. That discloses another customer's delivery note, total and share token, and the share token is itself the credential printed on the packing slip (db.ts:34-35).
findings.recommendation: Remove the swr rule from /api/orders/** and cache nothing that is scoped to a session. If the polling load is the concern, cache the courier position under a resource key that is not per-customer, or set the cache key to include the customer id explicitly.

triage.reason: The cached body carries the order note, the total and the share token (verbatim, [id].get.ts:14-19); the share token exists to grant access without signing in, so this is credential-bearing per-customer data.

The rule's pattern is '/api/orders/**', which matches exactly the two per-customer handlers; nothing in the same block or a more specific rule narrows it, and the sibling at line 32 shows the author knew how to exempt an area.

I could not establish from the tree what Nitro's swr cache key includes in the pinned version (nuxt ^3.14.1592, package.json:14). If that version's default key incorporates the session cookie, the finding collapses; the configuration in this repository sets no varies and no custom key, and no test or deployment artifact settles it. Per the triage contract this caps the finding at probable.

scope.established_by: Matched each of the four Nitro handler paths against the four routeRules patterns. '/api/orders/**' covers [id].get.ts and [id].patch.ts; only the GET is cacheable, so the PATCH is not in applies_to.
scope.narrowed_by: pantry-portal/nuxt.config.ts:32 - '/api/billing/**' is set to cache: false, so the webhook route is outside this finding. The create route at /api/orders is also outside the '/api/orders/**' pattern (no trailing segment), the same off-by-one prefix that produces F-08.

findings.title: The share token that grants access to an order without signing in is generated with Math.random
findings.unaided_label: pantry: share token from Math.random
findings.evidence: newShareToken (db.ts:36-43) draws twelve characters from a 33-character alphabet with Math.floor(Math.random() * alphabet.length). The doc comment on lines 34-35 states what the value is for: a handle printed on the packing slip so a household member can pull up the delivery window without signing in - an access credential. It is minted at insert time (db.ts:74), returned to the creating caller (index.post.ts:30 and [id].get.ts:19) and printed as a URL at db.ts:137. Math.random in V8 is xorshift128+, not a CSPRNG: its internal state is recoverable from a modest run of observed outputs, and successive tokens minted by the same process are drawn from the same stream.
findings.impact: An attacker who legitimately obtains a handful of tokens - by placing their own orders, which F-08 shows requires no account - can recover the generator state and predict the tokens issued to other customers around the same time, then open their share links. The 12-character length would be adequate against blind guessing; it is the predictability, not the length, that is the defect.
findings.recommendation: Use randomUUID() or randomBytes from node:crypto (already imported elsewhere in this codebase, 01.session.ts:1) and encode to the same alphabet, keeping at least 128 bits of entropy.

triage.reason: The comment at db.ts:34-35 declares the token an access handle for the delivery window, and the token is returned alongside the note and total in the order body; it is a credential, not an opaque display value.
The token is used as a bearer secret in a URL (db.ts:137), which is the form in which predictability is exploitable.

The route that consumes the token - /s/<token> on portal.pantrybox.example - is not in the tree, so I cannot show what it discloses to the bearer or whether it applies a second check. The generator weakness is fully established in code; the impact depends on a handler I was not given, which caps this at probable.

scope.established_by: grep for newShareToken: one definition, one call site, at the INSERT in insertOrder. It is the only token-shaped value the service mints; session MACs use node:crypto (01.session.ts:34) and idempotency keys come from the client.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it - every order created through any path gets a token from this generator.

findings.title: A shopper can advance their own order from draft to scheduled, which is the state the paid-charge webhook exists to set
findings.unaided_label: pantry: shopper can set status scheduled
findings.evidence: LOCKED_STATUSES at [id].patch.ts:5 contains out_for_delivery, delivered and cancelled, and line 12 rejects a patch that sets one of them with the message 'couriers set that status, not shoppers'. The enum the patch accepts (schemas.ts:3, via orderPatchSchema at line 25) has six members, so the three the customer may set are draft, scheduled and packing. scheduled is exactly the value the billing webhook writes on charge.succeeded, and it writes it only for an order still in draft: `SET status = 'scheduled', total_cents = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND status = 'draft'` (webhook.post.ts:42-43). The patch route applies no such transition guard - updateOrder (db.ts:94-111) writes whatever columns the patch names, scoped to the owner but not to any state machine.
findings.impact: The customer moves their own unpaid draft into the state the fulfilment pipeline treats as paid, without a charge and with total_cents left at the 0 that insertOrder wrote (db.ts:72). The states the designers protected are the ones the courier owns; the one that represents payment was left open.
findings.recommendation: Model the transition rather than the destination: allow a customer patch to change status only along shopper-owned edges (for example draft to cancelled), and reserve scheduled and packing to the webhook and the courier system. An allowlist of permitted from-to pairs beside the existing LOCKED_STATUSES set is the smallest fix.

triage.reason: The only checks on the path are the zod enum (schemas.ts:25), the LOCKED_STATUSES test ([id].patch.ts:12) and the ownership predicate inside updateOrder (db.ts:107). None of them constrains which state may follow which.
status is chosen by the caller from the six enum members; the enum bounds the vocabulary, not the authority to use a given word.
The second principal is the merchant: the customer is not escalating against another customer but against the business invariant that goods follow payment.

What the fulfilment side does with an order in scheduled is not in this tree - no worker, no picker, no courier integration was given. The transition gap is established in code; the consequence of reaching that state is inferred from the webhook's own use of it, which caps this at probable.

scope.established_by: Set difference between the six-member ORDER_STATUSES enum (schemas.ts:3) and the three-member LOCKED_STATUSES set, cross-checked against the status values the other two handlers write (webhook.post.ts:42 and :61) to see which of the remainder carries meaning the customer should not confer.
scope.narrowed_by: db.ts:107 - updateOrder carries AND customer_id = <session customer>, so a shopper can only do this to their own order, not to anyone else's.

findings.title: The adjustAmount signal rewrites the payout amount after the dual-approval threshold has been evaluated
findings.unaided_label: payout: adjustAmount signal skips approval
findings.evidence: The workflow reads the amount three times from a mutable local. Line 42 seeds `let amountMinor = input.amountMinor`; the signal handler at lines 54-56 assigns it whatever number arrives, with no validation and no re-evaluation of anything; line 93 tests `amountMinor > threshold` to decide whether two approvals are required; and lines 103-109 debit that same variable. Between the test on line 93 and the debit on line 103 the workflow awaits - either the approval condition on line 95 or nothing at all when the amount was under the threshold - and a signal delivered in that window mutates the variable the debit reads. Nothing re-checks the threshold after the signal, and the handler does not clamp the value or compare it against input.amountMinor.
findings.impact: Two ways round the treasury control. Submit a payout below the currency's dual-approval threshold (500.00 USD at lib/limits.ts:6), let the workflow pass line 93 without requiring approvals, then signal a larger amount - up to and beyond the 50,000.00 cap zod applies at submission (starter.ts:17) - and it is debited and sent to the rail with no second approver. Or signal a negative amount: postEntry's floor test at ledger.ts:38 computes balance - (-x) < floor, which passes trivially, and the UPDATE at line 42 subtracts a negative and credits the funding account instead of debiting it, with a ledger row labelled 'debit'.
findings.recommendation: Make the amount immutable after the approval decision. Either move the threshold evaluation to immediately before postEntry and recompute it from the current value, or have the signal handler reject any value that raises the required approval tier (and any value that is not a positive integer). Recording the amount that was approved, and refusing to debit a different one, is the invariant.

triage.reason: There is no compensating check between the signal and the debit. postEntry (ledger.ts:25-59) validates the funding balance against a floor and nothing about approvals; the approvals map is consulted only at payout.ts:95 and never again.

The signal payload is attacker-supplied and unvalidated end to end: starter.ts:55 casts the body with `as { amountMinor: number }` and passes body.amountMinor to handle.signal without a zod parse, in a handler that sits beside one that does parse (starter.ts:42).

The second principal is the treasury approval regime and the funding account it protects; the caller of the signal is not the party the dual-approval rule exists to constrain, and by design should not be able to set the amount alone.
The mutable variable is read by both the gate and the sink in the same function; no branch or condition confines the handler's effect to a narrower window.

scope.established_by: grep for adjustAmount across the tree returns four sites: the signal definition (payout.ts:35), the handler (payout.ts:54), the import and the send (starter.ts:6 and :57). Every read of amountMinor in the workflow was then listed in order and checked against the position of the await points.
scope.narrowed_by: starter.ts:83 binds the HTTP server to 127.0.0.1, so the signal route is reachable only from inside the pod. That bounds who can send it; it does not bound what the signal does, and it does not apply to a signal delivered through the Temporal client by any other holder of namespace access.

findings.title: A screening failure is swallowed and the payout proceeds as unscreened; the degraded flag that records it is read by nobody
findings.unaided_label: payout: screening failure swallowed
findings.class: Control that cannot fail / fail-open exception handling
findings.evidence: payout.ts:78-84 wraps screenBeneficiary in try/catch and the catch body assigns `screening = { blocked: false, listHits: [], degraded: true }` - the failure arm manufactures a clean result. The next statement, line 86, tests screening.blocked, which the catch has just set to false, so the payout continues. screenBeneficiary itself throws on any status at or above 400 (compliance.ts:32-34), so an unavailable or erroring screening service takes this path, and the proxy retry policy (payout.ts:16, maximumAttempts 3) exhausts into the same catch. The degraded field exists to record it: a grep across the tree shows it is written at compliance.ts:42 and payout.ts:83 and read nowhere - it reaches no branch, no query, no log and no ledger row.
findings.impact: Sanctions and watchlist screening is bypassed for the entire duration of any screening-service outage, silently. The comment on lines 81-82 offers the exception report as the compensating control, but the flag that would populate such a report is never consumed anywhere in this repository, so the batch that skipped screening is indistinguishable afterwards from the batch that passed it. Payments to listed beneficiaries clear.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: on a screening error, hold the payout (the manual-hold machinery already exists - releaseHold at compliance.ts:70) rather than continuing, or at minimum branch on degraded before postEntry and route those payouts to the approval path. If a degraded result must proceed, persist the flag with the payout so the morning report the comment refers to can actually be produced.

triage.reason: No layer re-screens. screenBeneficiary has one caller (payout.ts:79) and the only other compliance activity on the path, corridorVolume (line 90), counts corridor throughput and returns a number the workflow discards - it makes no decision.
The catch is unconditional production code with no environment guard.
Screening is not defence in depth here - it is the only sanctions control in the workflow, and the exception report that would back it up does not exist in the tree because nothing reads degraded.
This is not a control that could live outside the repository: the decision to proceed is taken here, in this catch block, whatever any external system holds.

scope.established_by: Applied WEB-27's caller test to the ScreeningResult fields: blocked is branched on at payout.ts:86; listHits and degraded are read nowhere (grep). The catch was then traced against screenBeneficiary's throw sites at compliance.ts:33.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. It is on the single path every schema-v2-and-above payout takes, ahead of every debit.

findings.title: Sanctions mode defaults to advisory, so a watchlist hit never blocks a payout unless an environment variable says otherwise
findings.unaided_label: payout: sanctions advisory by default
findings.evidence: config.ts:20 reads `sanctionsMode: process.env.SANCTIONS_MODE ?? 'advisory'`, and the interface comment at config.ts:6 states the contract: 'enforcing' blocks a payout on a list hit; 'advisory' records it for the morning review. The single consumer is compliance.ts:40, `blocked: listHits.length > 0 && config.sanctionsMode === 'enforcing'`. With the default in force the right-hand conjunct is false, so blocked is false for every beneficiary no matter how many list hits came back, and the workflow's only use of the result - payout.ts:86 - therefore never fires. listHits is returned and, as with degraded, read by nothing (grep: written at compliance.ts:37 and :41, never consumed).
findings.impact: A deployment that does not set SANCTIONS_MODE processes payouts to listed beneficiaries with the screening call made, the hits returned, and the decision discarded. Nothing in the tree records the hit either, so the 'morning review' the mode is named for has no input. Combined with F-14 the screening step has no path at all on which it stops a payment.
findings.recommendation: Default to enforcing and require an explicit opt-out for non-production environments, and persist listHits with the payout regardless of mode so that advisory actually records something. A default that turns a compliance control off is the wrong direction for the failure.

triage.reason: The rule asks whether the value is attacker-controlled; here the concern is the opposite direction - the default is the shipped value and it disables the control. FP-02's exculpation (a literal or placeholder) is precisely what makes this worse, not better.

config.ts is the production configuration module imported by the worker (worker.ts:3), the starter (starter.ts:4) and every activity. There is no separate production config that overrides it inside the repository.

SANCTIONS_MODE could be set to enforcing by a deployment manifest outside this tree. No such manifest, chart or written statement was provided, so per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. It does not cap this finding, because the defect I am reporting is the direction of the default itself, which is established at config.ts:20 regardless of what any one deployment sets.
The screening result governs whether money moves to a listed party; it is load-bearing, not a redundant layer.

scope.established_by: grep for sanctionsMode: declared at config.ts:7, assigned at config.ts:20, read at exactly one site, compliance.ts:40. That single read is the whole of the control's effect.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing in the repository narrows it. The corollary is that setting SANCTIONS_MODE=enforcing repairs this finding but not F-14, because the catch block bypasses the flag entirely.

findings.title: The payout API authenticates nobody: every route starts workflows, mutates amounts and reads any account's ledger on an unauthenticated request
findings.unaided_label: payout: no auth on the payout API
findings.evidence: The whole HTTP surface is the callback at starter.ts:36-80. It sets two response headers and then dispatches on method and URL; there is no authorization header read, no token verification, no session, no allowlist - a grep for 'authorization', 'token' or 'auth' in the file returns nothing. Three routes follow: POST /payouts starts a workflow (line 41-50), POST /payouts/{id}/amount signals the amount (line 53-60), and GET /accounts/{id}/entries returns ledger rows (line 63-71). The last takes accountId straight from the URL split at line 64 and passes it to entriesPage (ledger.ts:88), whose query filters on account_id = $1 and nothing else - no caller identity exists to scope it to.
findings.impact: Anyone who can reach the port initiates payouts, retargets the amount of a payout in flight (F-13) and enumerates the ledger of every funding account, including amounts, currencies and memo text. requestedBy is a self-asserted email from the body (starter.ts:19), so it is also the input to the dual-approval exclusion at payout.ts:48 - the caller chooses the identity the approval logic will refuse to count.
findings.recommendation: Put authentication in front of all three routes and derive the caller identity from it rather than from the body; scope /accounts/{id}/entries to accounts the caller may see. Keeping the loopback bind is right, but it is a network control and not an authorization one.

triage.reason: There is a second principal even on loopback: the comment at starter.ts:82 names an ops console sidecar in the same pod, so at least one other process shares the namespace, and the ledger data belongs to accounts the sidecar's users are not uniformly entitled to.
The absence of authentication is uniform across the handler; no route has a check that the others lack.

The exposure is intended to be bounded to the pod, and that bound is real - but FP-05 moves the finding to what sits behind the intended exposure rather than closing it, and what sits behind it is an unauthenticated ledger read and an unauthenticated amount signal.
No middleware layer exists: createServer receives the raw handler with nothing wrapped around it, and there is no proxy configuration in the repository.

scope.established_by: Enumerated every branch of the request handler (three routes plus the 404 fallback) and searched the file for any credential-reading construct; there is none. Cross-checked against the activity layer to see whether authorization is applied downstream - entriesPage, ledger.ts:88-95, applies none.
scope.narrowed_by: starter.ts:83 - server.listen(config.apiPort, '127.0.0.1') binds to loopback only, so the surface is not reachable from outside the pod. That is why this is medium and not high: it requires a co-located process, an SSRF into the pod, or any container sharing the network namespace.

findings.title: The rail reference doubles as the callback secret and the idempotency key, and is generated with Math.random
findings.unaided_label: payout: reference from Math.random used as a secret
findings.evidence: newReference (rails.ts:21-24) is `PO-${Date.now().toString(36)}-${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 12)}` uppercased. The doc comment directly above it, lines 17-20, states the security role: the rail quotes it back on its status callback, so it doubles as the callback secret. Two of the three components are not secret at all - the literal prefix and a base-36 timestamp, which narrows the search space to the moment of submission - and the third is Math.random, V8's xorshift128+, whose state is recoverable from observed outputs. The same value is sent as the idempotency-key header to the primary rail (rails.ts:30).
findings.impact: An attacker who can predict or brute-force a reference can forge the rail's status callback for that transfer, since the reference is what authenticates it. The timestamp component means a targeted guess needs only the submission second plus the random tail, and any party that has legitimately received references from this service (a beneficiary, a rail operator) has the outputs needed to attack the generator. Predictable idempotency keys additionally allow a third party to collide with an in-flight submission.
findings.recommendation: Generate the reference with randomUUID() or randomBytes from node:crypto. Better, stop overloading it: authenticate the rail's callback with a signature over the payload using a shared secret, and keep the reference as a non-secret correlation identifier.

triage.reason: The comment at rails.ts:19-20 declares the value a callback secret; it is not a display identifier.
This rule asks whether a value is attacker-controlled; the defect here is the opposite property - that a value which must be unguessable is guessable. The origin of the value is the generator itself.
The sink is a bearer-style secret carried in an inbound callback and in the idempotency-key header (rails.ts:30) - both forms in which predictability is directly exploitable.
No second factor authenticates the callback in this tree; there is no signature verification, no mTLS configuration and no allowlist for the rail's return path anywhere in the repository.

scope.established_by: grep for newReference: one definition and two call sites, one in each rail submission. Both put the value on the wire (line 31 and line 61) and submitPrimary additionally sets it as the idempotency-key header at line 30.
scope.narrowed_by: The correspondent rail submission (rails.ts:55-72) sends the reference in the body but sets no idempotency-key header, so the idempotency half of this finding applies only to submitPrimary; the callback-secret half applies to both.

findings.title: Dual approval counts distinct strings from an unauthenticated signal, not distinct approvers
findings.unaided_label: payout: approvals counted by string
findings.class: Business logic / weak separation of duties
findings.evidence: The approve handler at payout.ts:47-51 accepts an Approval object off the signal, applies one test - `if (approval.approver !== input.requestedBy)` - and keys the map on approval.approver. The release condition at line 95 is `approvals.size >= 2`, which counts map keys. Nothing verifies that approver names a real person, that the sender is that person, or that the two keys are two humans: 'a@x' and 'A@x', or 'a@x' and 'a@x ', are two keys. requestedBy, the only value excluded, is itself self-asserted from the request body (starter.ts:19, z.string().email()). The approver strings then become the audit trail: releaseHold is called with `approved by ${[...approvals.keys()].join(', ')}` at line 99, which is written to hold_note (compliance.ts:74).
findings.impact: The four-eyes control on payouts above the treasury threshold is satisfied by anyone who can send two signals with two different strings. The recorded justification for releasing the hold is those same unverified strings, so the ledger's account of who approved a large payment is attacker-authored.
findings.recommendation: Derive the approver identity from an authenticated credential presented with the signal, not from the payload; normalise and validate it against a directory of eligible approvers; and record the authenticated principal in hold_note. The requestedBy exclusion should compare authenticated identities too.

triage.reason: There is no authentication layer between a signal sender and the handler: starter.ts exposes no approve route, so the signal arrives through the Temporal client, and the worker (worker.ts:5-21) registers the workflow with no interceptor, no auth middleware and no payload verification.
approval.approver is an arbitrary string on the signal payload; the Approval interface (payout.ts:30-33) constrains nothing and no zod schema is applied to signals anywhere.
Separation of duties is by definition a control about two distinct principals; the finding is that the code cannot tell them apart.

The condition at line 48 does narrow the handler slightly - the requester's own string is refused - and that narrowing is exactly what I have accounted for: it stops the single most obvious self-approval and nothing else.

scope.established_by: grep for approve and approvals across the tree: the signal is defined at payout.ts:36, handled at :47, sized at :95 and serialised into the hold note at :99. No other file references either symbol, so the map's contents are established entirely by the handler.
scope.narrowed_by: payout.ts:93 - the approval requirement only engages for amounts above approvalThresholdFor(currency) (lib/limits.ts:21-23), and an unlisted currency returns Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, meaning payouts in a currency outside the eight-entry table never require approval at all. That is a widening rather than a narrowing, and I note it here because it is the same block.

findings.title: After a rail timeout the workflow submits the same transfer to a second rail with no idempotency key and no check that the first was rejected
findings.unaided_label: payout: correspondent fallback may double pay
findings.evidence: submitPrimary raises an error named RailUnavailable for status 503 and 504 only (rails.ts:43-47) - the statuses that mean the answer is unknown, not that the transfer was refused. The workflow's catch at payout.ts:125-131 reverses the debit and rethrows for every other error, and for RailUnavailable falls through to submitCorrespondent at line 133 with the same payoutId, beneficiary and amount. Nothing queries the primary rail for the transfer's actual state first. submitCorrespondent (rails.ts:55-67) sends no idempotency-key header, unlike submitPrimary which sets one at line 30. Above that, the activity proxy retries each activity up to three times (payout.ts:16), so a timeout inside submitPrimary itself re-runs the whole POST with a fresh reference from newReference (rails.ts:27), which is a new idempotency key for what the rail sees as the same payment.
findings.impact: A gateway timeout on a transfer the primary rail has already accepted produces a second, independent transfer through the correspondent rail: the beneficiary is paid twice and the funding account is debited once. The retry policy produces the same outcome within the primary rail, because a retried attempt presents a different idempotency key.
findings.recommendation: Derive the idempotency key from the payoutId rather than from a fresh random value, so a retry presents the same key; send it on the correspondent rail too; and before falling back, query the primary rail for the reference's status and treat unknown as requiring reconciliation rather than as free to re-send.

triage.reason: The idempotency key on submitPrimary (rails.ts:30) would be a compensating control if it were stable, but it is regenerated per attempt at line 27, and the correspondent path has none at all. No unique constraint or ledger guard covers the second submission: postEntry ran once, before the branch.
The trigger is a transport condition, not an attacker-supplied value.

The reading is direct: the catch on line 126 rethrows for every error whose name is not RailUnavailable, so RailUnavailable is the only condition that reaches line 133, and 503/504 are precisely the ambiguous outcomes.
A duplicated outbound payment is a direct financial loss, not a missing redundancy.

scope.established_by: Traced every throw site in rails.ts (lines 44-47, 48-50, 68-70) against the catch conditions in payout.ts:125-131 to establish which errors reach the fallback, then compared the two submission functions header by header to find the idempotency asymmetry.
scope.narrowed_by: payout.ts:126-130 - a genuine rejection (any status at or above 400 other than 503/504) does not reach the fallback: it reverses the debit and rethrows. The finding is confined to the two ambiguous statuses and to the proxy's own retries.

findings.title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin defaults to a wildcard on every payout API response
findings.unaided_label: payout: cors origin star default
findings.evidence: default_resolver.py flagged this line: `TABLE payout-orchestrator/src/config.ts:25 config can resolve to corsOrigin: process.env.PAYOUT_CORS_ORIGIN ?? '*'`. Reading confirms it: config.ts:25 supplies the fallback and starter.ts:37 writes it, unconditionally and before any routing, as `res.setHeader('access-control-allow-origin', config.corsOrigin)` - so it lands on all three route responses and on the 404 and the 400 error path as well. The header is emitted with no Vary and no credentials header.
findings.impact: Low as it stands. The API sets no cookies and reads no ambient credential, so a wildcard grants a cross-origin page nothing it could not obtain directly - but the surface it exposes is one that has no authentication at all (F-16), so if the loopback bind is ever relaxed, this header is what lets a page in a browser on that host read the ledger. Reported as the hardening item it is, not as the higher severity the wildcard on its own would suggest.
findings.recommendation: Default corsOrigin to the ops console's exact origin rather than to '*', and emit the header only for the routes a browser is meant to call.

triage.reason: Nothing narrows the header itself: it is set once, before dispatch, at starter.ts:37, so it applies to every response the server produces. What narrows the *impact* is the loopback bind and the absence of ambient credentials, which is why this is severity low rather than higher - the construct is exactly as wide as it reads.
The wildcard is a default, not a declared intent to be publicly readable; the interface at config.ts:12 names the field corsOrigin, implying a specific origin was expected.

Real but bounded: with no cookie, no Authorization requirement and a 127.0.0.1 bind (starter.ts:83), a cross-origin reader gains nothing an ordinary client on that host does not already have. Per FP-10 the severity drops and the finding is still written down - which is what this entry is.

scope.established_by: default_resolver.py named the declaration; grep for corsOrigin then established the single reader, at the top of the request handler where it is set before any branch.
scope.narrowed_by: payout-orchestrator/src/starter.ts:83 - the loopback bind means only a browser running on the pod's own network namespace can be induced to make the cross-origin request in the first place.

findings.title: The application-wide patient guard tests a path prefix that no route has, so the scope check and the care-link check never run
findings.unaided_label: labtrack: patient guard prefix never matches
findings.evidence: path_coverage.py reported: `DEAD GUARD '/api/results' guards nothing: no route starts with it [labtrack/labtrack/guards.py:72]`. Reading confirms the join. The guard is registered application-wide at app.py:46, guards=[require_patient_scope], so it runs for every request; its first statement pair, guards.py:71-73, is `path = connection.scope["path"]` then `if not path.startswith("/api/results"): return`. But the Litestar app is constructed with path="/api/v1" (app.py:44) and ResultsController declares path = "/results" (results.py:30), so the mounted routes are /api/v1/results/... Nothing in the application is served under /api/results, so the early return is taken on every request and lines 75-81 - the results:read scope requirement and the care-link test on patient_id - are unreachable.
findings.impact: Two controls are silently absent from every route. First, the scope requirement: effective_scopes (guards.py:54-66) is never consulted for reads, so a token minted for a client registered only for reports - billing-sync, settings.py:27 - reads lab results, and so does courier-hub. Second, and worse for a clinical system, the care-link test at guards.py:79-81 never fires, so an operator retrieves results for patients they have no care relationship with; the docstring at line 70 states that every result read must carry a care link, and none does. The org filter inside results_for_patient (store.py:39) still applies, so this is intra-organisation rather than cross-organisation - but the care link is precisely the intra-organisation control.
findings.recommendation: Compare against the mounted path, not the controller-relative one: startswith("/api/v1/results"), or better, derive the prefix from the app's path setting so a version bump cannot silently disable the guard again. Then add a test that asserts the guard raises for a token with no care link - a guard that cannot be made to fail is the shape that produced this.

triage.reason: No other layer performs either check. BearerAuth (guards.py:21-44) verifies the token's HMAC and expiry and does nothing with scopes or care_links; require_write and require_admin cover the write and delete routes only and test different properties; the store functions do not see care_links at all.

The reading that would make it benign - that connection.scope['path'] is controller-relative - is not how ASGI works: scope['path'] carries the full request path including the application's mount prefix. The tool's route inventory and the app.py:44 mount agree.
The guard's scope is not merely narrower than it looks - it is empty. There is no route it applies to.
app.py is the shipped wiring module; the guard registration and the prefix are both in it, in the same build.

scope.established_by: path_coverage.py's join of mounted route paths against guard prefixes flagged it; I then confirmed by composing app.py:44's path="/api/v1" with results.py:30's path="/results" and listing the three GET handlers that the guard was written to cover. The two write routes and the delete route carry their own working guards and are excluded.
scope.narrowed_by: labtrack/labtrack/services/store.py:39 - results_for_patient still filters on ordering_org = $2, so the organisation boundary survives on that one route. It does not survive on recent_by_panel, which is F-22.

findings.title: The recent-by-panel route returns every organisation's results for an assay, with no organisation predicate
findings.unaided_label: labtrack: panel recent leaks other orgs
findings.class: BOLA / cross-tenant disclosure of health data
findings.evidence: recent_by_panel (store.py:48-59) selects id, patient_id, panel_code, value_json, comment and resulted_at from results WHERE panel_code = $1 - one predicate, on a value the caller supplies. It takes no principal argument at all: the signature is (panel_code, order, limit), unlike its two siblings in the same file, results_for_patient (line 32) which takes principal and filters on ordering_org = $2 at line 39, and delete_result (line 113) which takes org_id and filters on it at line 115. The controller handler, results.py:42-49, likewise does not accept `request` and therefore cannot check the caller's organisation; contrast the handler immediately below it, results.py:51-56, which fetches by id and then compares row['ordering_org'] to request.scope['user']['org_id'] before returning.
findings.impact: Any holder of a valid token retrieves the most recent 500 results for any assay across the whole reference network, with patient_id, the full numeric result payload and the free-text clinician comment - other organisations' patients included. The docstring at line 49 describes the intent as the last N runs of one assay across the site; the query implements it across every site. This is bulk disclosure of identifiable health data, and F-21 removes the scope check that would at least have limited which tokens could ask.
findings.recommendation: Give the handler the request, pass the principal through, and add AND ordering_org = $2 to the query - the pattern the file already uses two functions above. If a cross-organisation view is genuinely needed for analyser QC, serve it de-identified and behind an explicit scope.

triage.reason: No mandatory layer applies an organisation filter: asyncpg is used directly through a raw pool (store.py:18-22), there is no ORM scope, no row-level security statement anywhere in the tree, and the one guard that could have gated this route is dead (F-21).
panel_code comes from the URL path (results.py:42-44) and is unconstrained; more to the point, the missing predicate is the organisation, which the caller never supplies at all.
The rows carry patient_id, value_json and the clinician comment from a lab result table - identifiable health data by any reading, and the same columns the per-patient route guards.
Nothing declares this endpoint public; it sits behind the same bearer middleware as the rest and its docstring describes a single site's dashboard.

scope.established_by: Listed every SELECT in store.py and checked each for an ordering_org predicate: results_for_patient has it (line 39), raw_result deliberately omits it and documents that callers apply their own check (line 63), delete_result has it (line 115). recent_by_panel is the one that neither has it nor delegates it, and its caller does not compensate.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The route requires only a valid bearer token; the limit is capped at 500 rows per call (results.py:49) but not the breadth.

findings.title: The report handler returns the cached HTML before it checks that the result belongs to the caller's organisation
findings.unaided_label: labtrack: report cache returned before the org check
findings.class: Authorization ordered after a cache read
findings.evidence: reports.py:22-33 in order: line 23 reads the cache, lines 24-25 return it if present, and only line 27-29 fetch the row and compare row['ordering_org'] to request.scope['user']['org_id']. The cache key is derived from the result id alone - render.py:40-41, 'report:' + sha256(result_id)[:32] - so it carries no organisation, no principal and no token. Once any authorised member of the owning organisation has viewed a report, put_report (reports.py:32, render.py:49-50) stores it for report_cache_seconds, 600 by default (settings.py:19), and every subsequent request for that result id inside the window is answered from line 25.
findings.impact: An operator in any organisation reads any other organisation's printable report - patient identifiers, panel, collected and resulted timestamps, every value row and the clinician comment - by requesting a result id during the ten-minute window after the legitimate viewer opened it. The 404 that the organisation check would produce is never reached. Result ids are the same identifiers returned by the create endpoint (results.py:69) and present in list responses, so they are not secret.
findings.recommendation: Fetch the row and check ordering_org first, then consult the cache; or key the cache on (org_id, result_id) so a cache hit cannot cross the boundary. The check must be on every path that returns content, not on the path that builds it.

triage.reason: The only authorization on this route is the comparison on line 28, and the cached return at line 25 precedes it. The application-wide guard that might have covered it is dead (F-21), and even had it fired it tests patient_id, which this route does not carry.
result_id is a path parameter (reports.py:21-22), supplied by the caller.
The cached document is the patient-facing report: title with panel code and patient id, collection and result timestamps, every value row and the comment (render.py:11-20, 29-37).
There is no reading in which line 25 is reached after line 28; the return is unconditional on a cache hit.

scope.established_by: Read the handler statement by statement and compared it against the sibling in results.py:51-56, which performs the same organisation check with no cache in front of it. The cache key construction was then read at render.py:40-41 to establish that the key does not vary by principal.
scope.narrowed_by: labtrack/labtrack/settings.py:19 - a cached report is only reachable for report_cache_seconds (default 600) after a legitimate view, so the exposure is a window per result rather than permanent. Nothing else narrows it.

findings.title: The attachment route joins a caller-supplied path onto the attachment root with no canonicalisation
findings.unaided_label: labtrack: attachment path traversal
findings.evidence: The route is declared @get("/attachments/{name:path}") at reports.py:35 - the :path converter matches slashes, so name arrives with separators intact. Line 37 builds `target = Path(settings.attachment_root) / name.lstrip("/")`. lstrip('/') removes leading separators only, which is what defeats the absolute-path case and nothing else: a name of ../../etc/passwd is untouched by it, and pathlib's / operator performs no normalisation. Line 38 tests only target.exists(), and line 41 returns target.read_bytes(). There is no resolve(), no relative_to check against the root, and no allowlist of extensions.
findings.impact: Arbitrary file read as the service account, over an authenticated but otherwise unrestricted route: /api/v1/reports/attachments/../../../../etc/passwd, or any application file, including the process environment through /proc/self/environ - which on this service exposes LABTRACK_TOKEN_KEY, the HMAC key that mints and verifies every bearer token (settings.py:17, guards.py:35). Recovering that key converts a read primitive into full token forgery with any org_id, role and care_links the attacker chooses. The response is labelled application/pdf but carries the bytes regardless.
findings.recommendation: Resolve and confine: `target = (Path(root) / name).resolve()` followed by an explicit `target.relative_to(Path(root).resolve())` inside a try, raising 404 on ValueError. Better, do not accept a path at all - store attachments under generated identifiers and look the name up in the database.

triage.reason: Nothing between the parameter and the read constrains it: the auth middleware (app.py:22) establishes who the caller is and inspects no path, and require_patient_scope returns early for this route as for every other (F-21).
name is the path parameter itself, matched with the :path converter that is chosen precisely to admit separators.
The sink is Path.read_bytes on line 41 and the bytes are returned to the caller in the response body; the declared media type does not constrain what was read.

lstrip('/') is sometimes mistaken for a traversal defence. It strips a prefix of slash characters and has no effect on an embedded '..' segment; pathlib's / does not normalise, so the dotdot survives to read_bytes.

scope.established_by: The file-sink enumeration over the tree returned this join as the only place a request value participates in a filesystem path in labtrack; the route table shows it is the only :path converter in the application.
scope.narrowed_by: labtrack/labtrack/app.py:22 - the route is inside the BearerAuth middleware's coverage (it is not in the exclude list), so a valid token is required. That is a precondition, not a mitigation: any registered client's token reaches it.

findings.title: The clinician comment is sanitised on one write path, not on the other, and the report template renders it unescaped
findings.unaided_label: labtrack: comment rendered raw
findings.evidence: render_report (render.py:29-37) escapes every field it interpolates except one: title through escape() at line 32, collected at 33, resulted at 34, and both the key and the value of every row through escape() in _rows at line 25 - and then line 36 passes comment=result['comment'] with no escape call, into a template whose comment slot at render.py:18 is `<section class="comment">{comment}</section>`. The result is served with media_type="text/html" (reports.py:21). Sanitisation was placed at write time instead, on one of the two writers: results.py:65 stores bleach.clean(data.comment, tags=ALLOWED_COMMENT_TAGS, strip=True). The other writer does not - bulk_import at store.py:90-110 builds its records with row.get("comment", "") at line 98 and inserts it verbatim, and its caller results.py:71-74 takes `data: list[dict]` with no schema at all.
findings.impact: A comment written through the nightly import path reaches the report as live HTML. The report is a patient-facing document served from the application's own origin, so script in it runs with the viewer's session - and the viewer is a clinician or portal user whose bearer token is what the application uses for every result read. The import route requires only a write scope (results.py:71), which clinic-desktop holds (settings.py:25), and the docstring's assurance that the interface engine has already parsed the rows out of HL7 is a statement about shape, not about safety.
findings.recommendation: Escape at render: `comment=escape(result["comment"])`, or run the bleach clean inside render_report so it applies to every stored value regardless of which writer produced it. One sanitisation point per output context, downstream of every writer.

triage.reason: The bleach call at results.py:65 is a control on one writer only; bulk_import reaches the same column without it, so no layer covers the sink. Naming results.py:65 as the compensating control would be exactly the wrong FP-01 answer that WEB-27 warns about.
The import payload is typed `list[dict]` (results.py:72) with no dataclass, no schema and no key validation; the comment value is whatever the caller sends.
The handler declares media_type="text/html" (reports.py:21) and the value lands between HTML tags, so the browser parses it as markup.
No CSP is set anywhere in the application - app.py constructs the Litestar instance with cors_config and middleware only - so nothing reduces the impact of execution.

scope.established_by: Listed the two writers of results.comment - insert_result via results.py:65 (sanitised) and bulk_import via store.py:98 (not) - and the one reader that renders it, render_report, reached from reports.py:31. writer_parity.py did not flag this entity; it was found by comparing the two INSERT statements in store.py side by side.
scope.narrowed_by: labtrack/labtrack/controllers/results.py:71 - the unsanitised writer is behind require_write, so the payload must come from a client registered for a write scope (clinic-desktop, settings.py:25). The sanitised route is not affected.

findings.title: The token endpoint is excluded from the rate limiter, leaving credential guessing unthrottled
findings.unaided_label: labtrack: token endpoint not rate limited
findings.evidence: RateLimitConfig at app.py:27-30 sets 120 requests per minute and excludes ['/health', '/api/v1/oauth']. The comment on lines 24-26 gives the reason - refresh storms after a network blip were tripping the limiter - and the exclusion is by path prefix, so it covers the whole TokenController (tokens.py:38, path = "/oauth"), including POST /token, which is the password grant. That handler (tokens.py:41-67) looks the operator up by username and client_id, verifies an argon2 hash (line 54) and mints a token; there is no attempt counter, no lockout, no backoff and no other limiter in the tree.
findings.impact: Unlimited password guessing against named operator accounts, from a single source, with no lockout. The distinct error paths do not leak much - both the unknown-row branch (line 51) and the mismatch branch (line 56) raise the same 'bad credentials' - but argon2 verification is the only cost imposed on an attacker, and a successful guess yields a token carrying scopes ['*'] (line 64) that expands to everything the client is registered for (guards.py:61-66).
findings.recommendation: Apply a limiter keyed on username and client_id to the token endpoint specifically, with lockout or exponential backoff, and exclude only the refresh path if the storm problem is real. Excluding an entire authentication controller to protect it from its own retry behaviour removes the control from the one route that most needs it.

It does not cap this finding at probable, because the defect asserted is the in-application exclusion at app.py:29, which is established from the file itself; the UNKNOWN bears on residual risk, not on whether the exclusion exists.
The endpoint's exposure is intended, but FP-05 moves the finding to what sits behind it - here, an unthrottled password grant.
