findings.title: The Sidekiq dashboard is mounted a second time as Rack middleware, outside the router and outside the platform-admin constraint that protects the first mount
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: sidekiq web mounted unauthenticated
findings.evidence: path_coverage.py reported: `DEAD GUARD '/internal/queues' guards nothing: no route starts with it [dispatch-workers/config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:34]` - no entry in config/routes.rb covers that prefix, which is the point. The same dashboard is mounted twice by two different mechanisms. In routes.rb:18-20 it is inside `authenticate :user, ->(user) { user.platform_admin? }` at /ops/sidekiq - the protected mount. In sidekiq.rb:34 it is inserted into the Rack middleware stack, which runs ahead of the router and is therefore not subject to any routing constraint, and line 30 immediately above it disables the dashboard's own session support with `Sidekiq::Web.set :sessions, false`. Devise is present (Gemfile:11, routes.rb:7) but the middleware mount is upstream of it.
findings.impact: The queue console is reachable without a session at all: queue contents and their arguments, the retry and dead sets, and the dashboard's own actions - retry, kill, delete and clear a queue. The job arguments on this instance are the partner event payloads and bulk-invite CSV rows, so reading them alone discloses member email addresses and org identifiers. The sidekiq-cron web extension is loaded too (routes.rb:4), which adds enqueue-now controls for scheduled jobs. Combined with F-31 and F-32, anything that can push onto the partner_bridge queue executes worker code, and this interface is a way to see and manipulate that queue.
findings.recommendation: Delete the middleware mount at sidekiq.rb:34 and keep the single router mount that carries the platform-admin constraint. If the NOC genuinely cannot present a session, put an authenticating proxy in front of that path rather than removing the check - and re-enable sessions on the dashboard so its own CSRF protection works.

triage.reason: Rack middleware runs before the router, so routes.rb:18's authenticate block cannot apply to it; that block governs the mount at line 19 only. No other middleware in the tree authenticates, and sessions are explicitly disabled for this app at sidekiq.rb:30.

The comment at sidekiq.rb:32-33 says the dashboards iframe this from inside the cluster, but no network policy, ingress rule or bind restriction appears anywhere in the repository; the path is served by the same Rails application that serves the public routes, on the same listener.

A cluster network policy could restrict /internal/queues to in-cluster callers. No such manifest was provided with the tree. Per FP-08 that is UNKNOWN, not HOLDS. It does not cap the finding: the defect asserted is that the second mount escapes the constraint the first one carries, which is established from these two files, and 'inside the cluster' is not a principal boundary in a system whose own partner bridge runs in someone else's VPC (inbound_event_worker.rb:4-5).
config/initializers/sidekiq.rb is loaded in every environment; the mount is unconditional, with no Rails.env guard.

scope.established_by: path_coverage.py's route-versus-guard join surfaced the orphan prefix; I then read both mount sites and established that one is a routing-constraint mount and the other is a middleware insertion, which is why the constraint does not reach it. The asymmetry between the two is decidable from the two files alone.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/config/routes.rb:18-20 narrows the *other* mount - /ops/sidekiq is genuinely behind authenticate + platform_admin? - which is what establishes that unauthenticated access was not the intent.

findings.title: update_role! applies no grant ceiling, so a partner event can set any membership to any role including platform_admin
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: update_role has no ceiling
findings.class: Privilege escalation / missing authorization on a sibling writer
findings.evidence: The class comment at invite_policy.rb:3-5 states the intent: a single place that decides whether an actor may put someone into an org at a given role, so the ceiling and the domain allow-list are applied once. invite! honours it - ROLES membership (line 21), the CEILING lookup against the actor's own role (lines 23-24), the verified-domain test (line 27) and the seat limit (line 29). update_role! (lines 36-41) keeps only the first of those: `raise Denied unless ROLES.include?(role)` and then `membership.update!(role: role, ...)`. It takes no actor argument at all, so no ceiling could be applied even in principle, and ROLES (line 7) includes platform_admin - the very role the comment on lines 9-10 says nobody may hand out from inside an org. Its caller is InboundEventWorker (inbound_event_worker.rb:17), which passes payload['role'] from a partner-supplied event.
findings.impact: A member.role_changed event promotes any existing membership in the target org to any role, including platform_admin. The comment at inbound_event_worker.rb:3-5 records two ingress routes for these events - the signed HTTP endpoint and a direct push onto the partner_bridge queue - and only the first applies EVENT_SCHEMA. Through the queue route the role string is entirely unconstrained; through the HTTP route it is constrained to viewer, dispatcher or supervisor (signed_payload.rb:21), which still lets a partner grant supervisor to an arbitrary address in the org with no ceiling test.
findings.recommendation: Give update_role! the actor and apply the same CEILING lookup invite! uses, and remove platform_admin from anything reachable through an org-scoped path. A policy object whose two entry points enforce different rules is not a single place that decides.

triage.reason: The gate is not applied by a layer neither method shows. The worker performs no authorization of its own - inbound_event_worker.rb:11-17 finds the org, finds the membership and calls straight through - and Sidekiq applies no policy. EVENT_SCHEMA narrows the value on one of the two ingress paths and is accounted for in narrowed_by; it is not a ceiling.

The two methods reach the same effect on the same column: invite! creates a Membership with a role, update_role! sets the role on an existing one. There is no reading in which the second is a lesser operation - it is the one that can raise an existing member to owner.
Both the method and its caller ship unconditionally; there is no environment guard on either.
payload['role'] originates outside the system by construction - the worker's own comment names a partner tenant as the source - and the queue ingress applies no schema to it.

scope.established_by: grep for update_role! returns the definition and exactly one caller. The asymmetry was established by reading the two public class methods of InvitePolicy side by side and listing which of the four checks in invite! each applies - the WEB-24 sibling comparison.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/lib/signed_payload.rb:21 - for events that arrive through SignedPayload.ingest! (the signed HTTP endpoint at routes.rb:15), the role is constrained to viewer, dispatcher or supervisor. That narrowing does not reach the queue ingress described at inbound_event_worker.rb:4-5 and sidekiq.yml:9-11, where the schema is never applied.

findings.title: A partner event updates the Org record with an arbitrary attribute hash
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: org settings mass assigned
findings.evidence: Line 22 is `org.update!(payload["org_settings"])` - the whole sub-hash from the event is handed to ActiveRecord's update!, which assigns every key it contains as an attribute. Strong parameters do not apply here: that is a controller concern and this is a worker, so nothing filters the keys. The comment on lines 20-21 asserts the settings block is already in the shape our Org model expects, which is an assumption about the well-behaved caller rather than a check. The Org attributes visible elsewhere in this tree are exactly the ones that matter: verified_domains and seat_limit are the two checks invite! relies on (invite_policy.rb:27 and :29), bridge_secret authenticates the signed HTTP ingest (signed_payload.rb:46) and the job-argument middleware (signed_payload.rb:60), and webhook_secret signs outbound deliveries (webhook_dispatch_worker.rb:19).
findings.impact: A partner rewrites the security-relevant attributes of the org record. Setting verified_domains disables the domain allow-list on invitations; setting seat_limit disables the seat cap; setting bridge_secret to a known value hands the attacker the ability to sign future ingest requests themselves, which converts a one-time queue write into durable authenticated access; setting webhook_secret makes the org's outbound webhook signatures forgeable. EVENT_SCHEMA constrains org_settings to retention_days and timezone (signed_payload.rb:24-27) on the HTTP path, and that constraint does not exist on the queue path the worker's own comment documents.
findings.recommendation: Assign an explicit allowlist in the worker - `org.update!(payload["org_settings"].slice("retention_days", "timezone"))` - rather than trusting the shape, and apply EVENT_SCHEMA to every ingress rather than only to the HTTP one. Attributes that carry secrets should not be assignable through any partner-driven path at all.

triage.reason: No mandatory layer filters the keys. EVENT_SCHEMA is applied by SignedPayload.ingest! (signed_payload.rb:47) and only there; jobs enqueued directly onto partner_bridge reach perform with whatever hash they carry, and JobSignatureMiddleware (signed_payload.rb:55-64) checks an HMAC when one is present and never inspects the payload's keys.
The partner tenant and the org whose record is rewritten are distinct principals; the worker's comment places the bridge process in the partner's own VPC.
The attributes reachable include two secrets and the two limits that the invitation policy enforces, established from their use in three other files in this tree.
payload is the job argument, supplied by whichever ingress produced it; on the queue path nothing constrains it.

scope.established_by: Enumerated the three branches of the event case statement and checked what each does with caller-supplied values: member.role_changed calls the policy (F-28), shipment.scanned resolves through a frozen lookup table (ruled out), and org.settings_updated passes a hash straight to update!. The reachable attribute names were established by grepping for org.<attr> uses across the tree.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/lib/signed_payload.rb:24-27 - events arriving through the signed HTTP endpoint have org_settings constrained to retention_days (30..3650) and timezone. That narrowing applies to routes.rb:15 only, not to the partner_bridge queue ingress.

findings.title: The bulk invite worker writes memberships directly, bypassing every check the invitation policy exists to apply
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: bulk invite bypasses the policy
findings.class: Privilege escalation / policy bypass by a sibling writer
findings.evidence: InvitePolicy's comment (invite_policy.rb:3-5) names the memberships controller and the invite worker as the two callers that both go through invite! so the ceiling and the domain allow-list are applied once. This worker does not call invite!. Lines 34-38 build the record itself - `Membership.find_or_initialize_by(org: org, email: email)`, then assign role, invited_by and state, then save! - and the only validation in the loop is line 32, `next unless InvitePolicy::ROLES.include?(role)`. ROLES (invite_policy.rb:7) contains platform_admin. So of the four checks invite! performs, this path keeps the role-name check and drops the CEILING lookup, the verified-domain test and the seat limit. The one authorization present is line 17, `return unless actor.owner_of?(org)` - which establishes the actor is an owner, and CEILING['owner'] (invite_policy.rb:12) grants viewer, dispatcher, supervisor and owner, deliberately not platform_admin.
findings.impact: An org owner uploads a CSV with role platform_admin and the worker writes it. The CEILING table exists to make platform_admin ungrantable from inside an org and this path makes it grantable. The same rows also bypass the verified-domain allow-list, so memberships can be created for addresses at any domain, and the seat limit, so the paid seat cap does not apply to bulk uploads.
findings.recommendation: Call InvitePolicy.invite!(actor: actor, org: org, email: email, role: role) inside the loop and rescue InvitePolicy::Denied per row to collect failures for the summary mail, rather than reimplementing a subset of it. If bulk performance is the reason for the direct write, move the batching inside the policy - not the policy inside the worker.

triage.reason: No model-level layer restores the checks: the ceiling, the domain list and the seat limit exist only as Ruby in InvitePolicy.invite!, and Membership is written here through find_or_initialize_by/save! with nothing in between. There is no validation in the tree that would reject a platform_admin membership at the model.

The two paths reach the same effect: a Membership row for an org, an email and a role. The header comment on this very worker (lines 3-5) claims the controller has already validated the upload for shape, which is explicitly not the same as authorising the roles it names.
row['role'] comes from the uploaded CSV; the only constraint on it is membership of ROLES, which admits platform_admin.

The loop is the worker's main path. The development-only branch above it (lines 19-22) is a separate matter and is ruled out on FP-04 in provenance.ruled_out; this finding is about lines 25-40, which carry no environment guard.

scope.established_by: Listed every writer of Membership in the tree - invite_policy.rb:31 (create!, full checks), invite_policy.rb:45 (create!, no checks, dev-gated), invite_policy.rb:39 (update!, F-28) and bulk_invite_worker.rb:38 (save!, this finding) - and compared the checks applied on each edge. writer_parity.py returned no flag for this entity; the comparison was done by reading.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/app/workers/bulk_invite_worker.rb:17 - `return unless actor.owner_of?(org)` confines the bypass to org owners acting on their own org. That is what makes it an escalation from owner to platform_admin rather than an open write; it does not confine the domain or seat-limit bypasses at all.

findings.title: The job signature middleware verifies a payload only when the payload itself carries a signature field
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: signature skipped when _sig absent
findings.class: Control that cannot fail / optional signature
findings.evidence: The middleware's whole decision is line 58: `if payload.is_a?(Hash) && payload.key?("_sig")`. When the key is present the HMAC is verified against the org's bridge_secret and a mismatch raises (lines 59-60). When the key is absent, the conditional is skipped and line 62 yields - the job runs unverified. The attacker chooses whether the key is present, so the control is optional to the party it constrains. The comment at lines 53-54 states the intent - re-check the HMAC carried in a job's own arguments, for jobs pushed to Redis rather than posted over HTTP - which is exactly the ingress that has no other authentication.
findings.impact: The only integrity control on the partner_bridge queue is skipped by omitting one field. Anything that can write to Redis enqueues an InboundEventWorker job with no _sig and the worker executes it, which reaches the privilege escalation in F-28 and the mass assignment in F-29 with no signature at all. The same omission covers every other job class the middleware sees.
findings.recommendation: Invert the default: require _sig on the queues that carry externally-originated jobs and raise SecurityError when it is missing, rather than when it is present and wrong. An allowlist of job classes exempt from verification is the right shape if internal producers cannot sign.

triage.reason: No other verification covers the queue path. SignedPayload.ingest! (line 45) verifies the HTTP path and enqueues a job that will itself carry no _sig; nothing in InboundEventWorker or Sidekiq re-checks provenance.
The permissive arm is the default arm of a production code path, not a test double or a flagged branch.
This is not defence in depth. On a queue that a partner process writes to directly, per sidekiq.yml:9-11, it is the only authentication the payload gets.
There is no reading in which an absent key means the job was verified: the guard clause is a presence test and the else branch is the yield.

scope.established_by: grep for JobSignatureMiddleware: defined here, registered once at sidekiq.rb:17. Applied WEB-27's caller test to SignedPayload.verify! - it is called at line 46 inside ingest!, where the result governs the flow, and at line 60 inside a conditional the caller controls.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:17 - the middleware is added to the server chain only when VERIFY_JOB_ARGS is true, and line 11 defaults it to off. So in a default deployment this control is not merely skippable, it is not installed; that default is F-32.

findings.title: Job argument verification is off by default
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: job verification off by default
findings.evidence: sidekiq.rb:11 reads `VERIFY_JOB_ARGS = ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS", "off") == "on"` and line 17 registers the signature middleware only `if VERIFY_JOB_ARGS`. The comment on lines 9-10 states the reasoning - verification is opt-in per environment while the bridge finishes rolling out signing - so the fail-open is deliberate and time-boxed by intent, with nothing in the repository enforcing the time box. sidekiq.yml:9-11 documents the queue this protects: the partner bridge writes jobs straight onto partner_bridge with the Sidekiq client protocol, drained by the same pool as everything else.
findings.impact: In a default deployment the server middleware chain contains no signature check at all, so the partner_bridge queue accepts any job any Redis writer enqueues. That is the same reachable consequence as F-31 - InvitePolicy.update_role! and org.update! driven by an unauthenticated payload - arrived at one step earlier.
findings.recommendation: Default to on and let a specific environment opt out while the rollout completes, so the insecure state is the one that must be chosen explicitly. Pair it with the fix in F-31 so that turning it on actually rejects unsigned payloads.

triage.reason: The initializer is loaded in every environment and the default applies to all of them; there is no production branch that sets it on.

SIDEKIQ_VERIFY_ARGS may be set to on by a deployment manifest outside the repository. None was provided, so per FP-08 the answer is UNKNOWN rather than HOLDS. It does not cap the finding, because what is asserted is the direction of the default at line 11, which is established from the file.
There is no second authentication on the queue path to which this could be redundant; Redis is protected only by the credential in the connection string, which is F-33.
The concern is not an attacker-supplied value but a shipped default that removes a control.

scope.established_by: grep for VERIFY_JOB_ARGS: assigned at line 11, read at exactly one site, line 17, where it decides whether the middleware joins the server chain.
scope.narrowed_by: dispatch-workers/config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:13 - the chain is configured inside configure_server, so this affects the worker processes that execute jobs; the client configuration at line 26 is unaffected, which is consistent with the control being about inbound execution.

findings.title: The Redis connection string carries a default password in source
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: redis password in source
findings.evidence: sidekiq.rb:7: `REDIS_URL = ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL", "redis://:sidekiq@localhost:6379/1")`. The fallback embeds the password `sidekiq` - the service's own name - and is used by both the server (line 14) and the client (line 27) configurations. It is a default rather than the only value, and it points at localhost, which is what keeps this low.
findings.impact: A deployment that does not set SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL authenticates to Redis with a guessable password committed to the repository. Given F-31 and F-32, write access to that Redis instance is job execution on the partner_bridge queue, so the credential is worth more than it looks.
findings.recommendation: Use ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL") with no default so a missing value fails at boot, and keep credentials out of source entirely.

triage.reason: It is not a placeholder of the ${VAR} or changeme kind - it is a syntactically complete credential that a running process will actually present.
The initializer ships in every environment and the fallback has no environment guard.

Real but bounded: the host component is localhost, so the credential is only useful to something already on the box or to a deployment that inherited the default with a networked Redis. Per FP-10 the severity drops to low and the finding is written down rather than deleted.

scope.established_by: Enumerated config/initializers/sidekiq.rb key by key per COV-02 (six statements: the require block, REDIS_URL, VERIFY_JOB_ARGS, the server chain, the death handler, the two mounts) rather than reading it for its one obvious problem - which is how F-27, F-32 and this were all found in the same 34-line file.
scope.narrowed_by: The literal host in the default is localhost:6379, so the credential is presented to a loopback service unless the deployment overrides the whole URL - in which case it presents whatever that override carries and this default is unused.

findings.title: The webhook dispatcher posts to a URL taken from the job arguments with no scheme, host or address validation
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: webhook url unvalidated
findings.evidence: perform takes (org_id, event_id, url) at line 14 and hands the third argument straight to Faraday.new(url: url) at line 21, then posts the event body to it (lines 24-28). There is no allowlist, no scheme check, no DNS or address inspection and no redirect policy anywhere in the file or in the tree. The class comment at lines 5-6 states where the value can come from: the subscriber may be one of the org's registered endpoints or a one-shot callback the partner asked us to hit - the second of which is a partner-supplied URL by construction.
findings.impact: The worker makes the request from inside the application's network position, so a partner-chosen URL reaches loopback services, cluster-internal addresses and the cloud metadata endpoint, with the event payload as the POST body and an org-scoped HMAC header attached (line 26). The response status is persisted on the event (line 33), which gives a coarse read-back channel for probing internal hosts.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the host and reject non-public addresses before connecting, restrict the scheme to https, and disable redirects (or re-validate after each hop). For one-shot callbacks, require the partner to pre-register the destination host so the allowlist is the durable object rather than the request.

triage.reason: Nothing validates the URL on the path to the sink: the worker performs no check, Faraday applies none by default, and no egress proxy, network policy or configuration constraining outbound traffic appears anywhere in the repository.

The enqueuing site is not in the tree - a grep for WebhookDispatchWorker returns only this file, so the controller or service that supplies url was not given to me. The class comment states a partner-supplied one-shot callback is one of the intended sources, which is in-repository evidence for attacker control, but it is a comment and not a call site. Per the triage contract this caps the finding at probable; what would settle it is the enqueuer.
The second principal is the internal network the worker sits in versus the partner who names the destination.

scope.established_by: The outbound-client enumeration over the tree returned one HTTP client taking a variable destination (this one); the other two outbound calls, in payout-orchestrator, take base URLs from configuration constants. grep established that no other file in dispatch-workers references this worker.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing in the repository narrows it. The signature header at line 26 is computed from the org's own secret, so the request is authenticated to the destination - which does not constrain which destination it is.

findings.title: The manifest renderer writes the generated PDF to a filename taken from the job arguments
findings.unaided_label: dispatch: manifest filename traversal
findings.evidence: Line 18 takes `filename = args["filename"].presence || "#{manifest.reference}.pdf"` - the caller's value when present, a derived name otherwise. Line 26 is `target = SPOOL.join(filename)`, where SPOOL is Rails.root.join('tmp','manifests') (line 13). Pathname#join follows the same rule as File.join's absolute-path handling in Ruby: joining an absolute path discards the receiver, so a filename of /etc/cron.d/x resolves outside the spool entirely, and a relative ../../ sequence walks out of it. Line 27 then calls FileUtils.mkdir_p(File.dirname(target)), which creates whatever directory the traversal names, and line 29 writes the PDF there. The path is finally persisted on the manifest at line 37.
findings.impact: Arbitrary file creation and overwrite as the worker's user, anywhere the process can write, with attacker-influenced content in the body (the manifest reference and each stop's address_line and window are rendered into the document at lines 30-33). Overwriting a file in a directory that something else executes or reads on a schedule turns that into code execution; at minimum it is destruction of arbitrary files, since Prawn::Document.generate truncates its target.
findings.recommendation: Never accept a path component from the caller: derive the name from the manifest (the fallback on line 18 already shows the right shape) or sanitise with File.basename and reject anything containing a separator, then assert that the expanded target is still inside SPOOL before writing.

triage.reason: No canonicalisation or containment check exists between line 18 and the write: no File.basename, no expand_path comparison, no allowlist. The mkdir_p on line 27 actively cooperates with the traversal by creating the parent.

The enqueuer is not in the tree - a grep for ManifestRenderWorker returns only this file, and routes.rb:11 shows a manifests controller exists but its source was not given. So I cannot show that args['filename'] is caller-controlled rather than server-generated. The parameter exists and is preferred over the derived name, which is evidence but not proof. Per the triage contract this caps the finding at probable; the manifests controller would settle it.
Pathname#join with an absolute argument returning the argument is documented Ruby behaviour, not a misreading; and the relative traversal case does not depend on it at all.

scope.established_by: The filesystem-sink enumeration returned two path constructions in dispatch-workers, both in this worker (the spool join and the mkdir_p on its dirname). The sibling value on line 17, args['page'], is coerced with to_i and is ruled out separately.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The fallback on line 18 is only taken when the argument is blank, so supplying any value takes the caller-controlled branch.

findings.title: The admin function is published with no authentication middleware while its sibling function has one
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: adminApi has no auth
findings.class: Missing authentication on an administrative surface
findings.evidence: Two express apps are built in the same file with the same helper available to both. The public one registers both middlewares: `api.use(corsMiddleware)` then `api.use(requireIdToken)` (index.js:42-43). The administrative one registers only the first: `adminApi.use(corsMiddleware)` at line 72, and there is no second use() before its routes at lines 74 and 79 or after them. requireIdToken (lines 17-29) is the only credential check in the file. Both are exported as onRequest functions (lines 110-111) and both are published: firebase.json:6-7 rewrites /api/** to api and /admin/** to adminApi, so the admin app is served from the same public hosting site as the rest of the application.
findings.impact: GET /admin/orgs/{orgId}/members returns every member document of any organisation to an anonymous caller (line 75-76 reads the collection with the Admin SDK and returns each document's full data, so whatever member records hold - names, emails, roles - is disclosed). POST /admin/orgs/{orgId}/seats rewrites the seatLimit of any organisation (line 80). Neither route checks a token, a membership or a role, and orgId is taken from the path.
findings.recommendation: Add `adminApi.use(requireIdToken)` and then an explicit administrator check - the membership lookup pattern the sibling route already uses at lines 47-50 - before either handler. A second express app is not a second trust boundary unless it is given one.

triage.reason: No layer in front authenticates: the hosting rewrite at firebase.json:7 routes to the function directly, onRequest applies no auth of its own, and the Firestore security rules do not apply here at all because the handlers use the Admin SDK (index.js:7-8), which bypasses rules by design.

The two apps reach comparable effects on the same data - one reads org notes with a membership check, the other reads org members and writes org configuration with none. The difference between them is one missing use() call on line 72.
adminApi is exported at index.js:111 and rewritten to at firebase.json:7; it is in what ships, not behind a flag.
The caller is anonymous on the public internet and the data belongs to named organisations; the boundary is as clear as it gets.

scope.established_by: Listed both express apps' middleware registrations and every route on each, then joined against firebase.json's rewrite table to confirm both are published. The two adminApi routes are the ones with no credential check; the two api routes both sit behind requireIdToken.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. Neither handler applies a membership, role or ownership test of its own that would compensate for the missing middleware.

findings.title: The org-wide note export callable checks neither authentication nor membership and runs with the Admin SDK
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: export callable by anyone
findings.class: Missing authorization on a privileged export
findings.evidence: The handler body (index.js:88-101) validates one thing: that orgId is non-empty (lines 89-92). It never reads request.auth, which is the field a v2 onCall carries the verified caller in, and it never consults the caller's profile. It then reads up to 5000 documents from orgs/{orgId}/notes through the Admin SDK instance created at line 8 - which bypasses the Firestore rules entirely - and returns their id, ownerId, status, title and body as CSV. The comment at lines 84-87 states the intent and the reason for the privilege: it runs with the Admin SDK because the export spans every inspector's notes in the org. The contrast is in the same file: the /notes/recent route establishes the caller's uid from a verified token and checks org membership before reading the same collection (lines 47-50).
findings.impact: Anyone who can invoke the callable - v2 onCall accepts unauthenticated invocations unless the handler rejects them - exports every field note of any organisation, including the full body text, by naming the org id. That is the whole content of the product for that tenant, retrieved with a single call and no credential.
findings.recommendation: Reject the call when request.auth is absent, then check that request.auth.uid's profile lists orgId in its orgs array - the same three lines the recent-notes route already contains - before touching the collection. Consider requiring an admin role as well, given the export spans every inspector.

triage.reason: The Firestore rules cannot compensate: admin.firestore() (index.js:8) is a privileged client and rules do not apply to it. There is no other layer - onCall's own contract is that the handler decides.
The caller and the org whose notes are exported are distinct principals; the function is published to the internet as a callable endpoint.
The exported rows carry ownerId, title and body of inspection field notes - the tenant's operational data, and the same collection every other rule in this service tries to protect.
orgId is String(request.data?.orgId) with only an emptiness test; unlike the express routes it does not even pass through normalizeRequest's character filter.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all five exported entry points in the file (api's two routes, adminApi's two, and this callable) and checked each for a credential read and a membership check. /notes/recent has both; /notes/:noteId/seal has the credential only; the two admin routes and this callable have neither.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The 5000-document limit at line 94 bounds the size of one export, not who may request it or which org they may name.

findings.title: The seal route writes audit documents at a client-chosen id for a client-chosen org, into a collection the rules declare immutable
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: seal writes audits for any org
findings.class: Forgeable audit trail / missing object-level authorization
findings.evidence: The handler (index.js:59-69) takes orgId and seq from the request body through normalizeRequest, composes the document id as `${orgId}_${seq}` (line 61) and calls db.doc(`audits/${auditId}`).set({...}) at line 62. set() without merge replaces an existing document, so an id that already exists is overwritten. Nothing checks that the caller is a member of orgId - the sibling route ten lines above does exactly that check (lines 47-50) - and nothing checks that noteId belongs to that org or to the caller. The rules file declares the collection's intent at firestore.rules:50-53: an immutable trail written by the audit function with the Admin SDK, `allow write: if false`, which stops clients writing directly and is precisely why this function's write is the only way in.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user forges audit entries attributing a seal to themselves for any org and any note, and - because seq is theirs to choose and set() overwrites - deletes or rewrites existing audit records by colliding with their ids. An audit trail that the application's own rules protect as immutable is fully writable through the one function that reaches it. The sealedBy and sealedAt fields are server-controlled (lines 65-66), which makes the forged records look authentic.
findings.recommendation: Check membership of orgId and ownership of noteId before writing, derive the document id from the note rather than from client input, and use create() (or a transaction that refuses an existing document) so a collision fails instead of overwriting.

triage.reason: requireIdToken (index.js:43) establishes who the caller is and nothing more; the Firestore rules do not apply because the write goes through the Admin SDK client at index.js:8, which is the reason the collection is client-unwritable in the first place.

orgId and seq come from req.body through normalizeRequest (index.js:32-39), which strips characters outside [A-Za-z0-9_-] from orgId and coerces seq to a number - constraints on form, not on entitlement. noteId is the raw path parameter.
The rules file gives the collection a read audience of admins and auditors (firestore.rules:52) and declares it immutable; it is evidentiary data by the application's own account.
Firestore's set() without a merge option replaces the document; there is no reading in which the existing record survives.

scope.established_by: Compared the two routes on the same express app: /notes/recent reads profile and tests org membership before its query (lines 47-50); /notes/:noteId/seal performs neither before its write. The collection's intended write path was then confirmed against firestore.rules:51-53.
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/functions/index.js:43 - the route is behind requireIdToken, so a valid Firebase ID token is required. Given F-39, obtaining one is self-service registration (auth.js:35-39), so this narrows the finding very little.

findings.title: Users may write their own profile document, and the profile's role and orgs fields are what every other rule authorizes against
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: profile self-write sets role
findings.class: Privilege escalation through a self-writable authorization record
findings.evidence: firestore.rules:31 is `allow write: if request.auth.uid == uid` - the owner may write every field of their own profile. The profile is not a display record: the two helper functions the rest of the file authorizes with read from it. role() at lines 14-16 returns profile().role, and memberOf(orgId) at lines 18-20 returns `orgId in profile().orgs`. Those helpers gate the org documents (line 42 read, line 43 write for role() == 'admin'), the entire org subtree (line 46), and the audit trail (line 52, admins and auditors). The document's shape is established by the client that creates it: auth.js:24-30 writes role: DEFAULT_ROLE and orgs: [orgId], and registration is open self-service (auth.js:35-39, createUserWithEmailAndPassword).
findings.impact: Any user registers, then writes their own profile with role 'admin' and orgs containing every org id they wish. That grants read and write on those org documents (rules line 43), read and write on everything beneath them including all inspectors' notes (line 46), and read of the audit trail (line 52). It also satisfies the membership check the notes/recent function performs (index.js:48), since that function reads the same profile document. One self-write is full tenant compromise across every org whose id is known, and org ids are visible in note documents (notes.js:32 stores orgId on every note).
findings.recommendation: Constrain the write to the fields the user owns and freeze the authorization fields: `allow update: if request.auth.uid == uid && request.resource.data.role == resource.data.role && request.resource.data.orgs == resource.data.orgs`, with role and orgs set only by an administrative function using the Admin SDK. An authorization record that its subject can write is not an authorization record.

triage.reason: No layer above the rules constrains this write: the web client writes profiles directly through the Firestore SDK (auth.js:31), not through a function, so there is no server-side code path to enforce anything. The functions that read the profile (index.js:47) trust what they find.
The document contents are supplied by the client SDK call; nothing in the rule constrains request.resource.data.

The rule is narrow in one dimension - a user may write only their own profile - and that narrowing is exactly what does not help, because their own profile is the input to every authorization decision about everyone else's data.
The second principal is every other inspector and every org: the escalation reaches their notes and the audit trail.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all fourteen allow statements in the rules file and traced which of them evaluate role() or memberOf(), both of which resolve through profile(). Five sites depend on the profile document; all five are listed. The functions-side dependency was found by grepping for the profiles path in index.js.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. firestore.rules:29-32 has no field-level condition, no immutability clause and no create-versus-update distinction.

findings.title: A recursive wildcard grants every org member full write over the whole org subtree, overriding the per-owner note rule
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: org wildcard rule beats note ownership
findings.evidence: firestore.rules:45-47 nests `match /{document=**} { allow read, write: if memberOf(orgId); }` inside the orgs match. The recursive wildcard covers every document at any depth beneath an org, which is where the application actually stores notes: notes.js:18-20 builds the collection as collection(db, 'orgs', orgId, 'notes'), and every write path in that file - createNote (line 31), updateNote (line 45), deleteNote (line 52) - addresses that subcollection. The ownership rule that expresses the intended model, `allow read/update/delete: if resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid` at lines 36-38 with the comment at line 34 that a field note belongs to the inspector who took it, is written against the top-level /notes/{noteId} path, which no code in the tree reads or writes. So the ownership rule governs an unused collection and the wildcard governs the real one.
findings.impact: Any member of an org reads, rewrites and deletes every other inspector's field notes in that org, including the body text and the lastAttachment link. The stated model - a note belongs to the inspector who took it - is not enforced anywhere that data actually lives. Combined with F-39, which lets any user become a member of any org, this is the reach that turns a self-granted membership into full access to another tenant's notes.
findings.recommendation: Replace the recursive wildcard with explicit matches per subcollection, and put the ownership condition on the path the application uses: `match /orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}` with read allowed to members and update/delete restricted to resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid. Then delete the dead top-level /notes rule so it cannot be mistaken for the live one.

triage.reason: The web client writes notes directly through the Firestore SDK (notes.js:31, 45, 52), so the rules are the only enforcement layer; there is no function in the path that could apply ownership.

This is the rule the FP-11 question is properly asked of, and the answer is that nothing narrows it: the recursive wildcard's condition is membership alone, and no more specific match for orgs/{orgId}/notes exists to take precedence. In Firestore, rules are permissive-union across matching paths, so an ownership rule elsewhere could not restrict this one even if it were on the right path.
Field notes carry title, body, siteRef and an attachment URL per inspection (notes.js:31-40); the whole product's data.
Nothing declares org-wide write as intended; the neighbouring comment at line 34 declares the opposite model.

scope.established_by: Joined the rules file's path patterns against the collection paths the client code actually addresses. Every Firestore path constructed in web/src (notes.js:19, notes.js:45, notes.js:52, share.js:20, auth.js:18) was listed and matched: the note paths fall under the orgs wildcard, none falls under top-level /notes.
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/firestore.rules:19 - the condition is membership of that specific org, so a member of org A does not reach org B's subtree through this rule alone. F-39 is what removes that constraint.

findings.title: The storage update rule requires only that the caller is signed in, dropping the ownership, size and content-type conditions its create sibling applies
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: storage update rule wide open
findings.class: Missing authorization and upload validation on one verb
findings.evidence: The four verbs on the same path are declared together and three of them agree: read (line 12) and delete (line 22) both require `noteOwner() == request.auth.uid`, and create (lines 14-17) requires that plus `request.resource.size < 15 * 1024 * 1024` and `request.resource.contentType.matches('image/.*|application/pdf')`. update (line 20) requires `request.auth != null` and nothing else. The comment above it explains the intent - re-uploading a photo after the inspector rotates or crops it - which is an argument for allowing the owner to update, not for dropping every condition. In Firebase Storage, update is the verb an overwrite of an existing object takes, so the create rule's conditions do not apply to it.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user overwrites any attachment on any note in any org - evidence substitution on inspection records, which for a field-notes product is the integrity property that matters most. The size cap is gone, so an overwrite is unbounded, and the content-type restriction is gone, so an object whose siblings are constrained to images and PDFs can be replaced with HTML or JavaScript served from the storage bucket's own origin, and the URL is already published into the note document by attachPhoto (notes.js:63) for anyone who reads the note to follow.
findings.recommendation: Give update the same conditions as create: owner, size and content-type. There is no reason for a re-upload to be less constrained than the original upload.

triage.reason: Uploads go directly from the browser to Storage (notes.js:60-61, uploadBytes), so the rules are the only control; no function mediates the write.

The four verbs govern the same object path and are written in the same block, which is what makes the asymmetry decidable here rather than inferred. Storage's create/update split is precisely overwrite-versus-first-write, so this is the overwrite rule.

The path pattern narrows it to note attachments, which is the whole of the service's file storage; within that pattern the condition is any authenticated user, and the exports path at lines 25-27 is separately closed with `if false`.
The objects are inspection photographs and PDFs attached to field notes - the evidentiary content of the product.

scope.established_by: Enumerated all five allow statements in storage.rules and listed the conditions on each, per COV-02. Four are on one path pattern and one closes the exports path; the update statement is the only one of the four that omits noteOwner().
scope.narrowed_by: fieldnotes/storage.rules:6 - the rule applies only to the orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}/{fileName} pattern, so it does not reach the exports prefix, which is closed to everyone at line 26.

findings.title: The shared-note view assigns the note body to innerHTML
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: innerHTML on note body
findings.evidence: share.js:39 is `article.innerHTML = note.body`, where note is the raw Firestore document read at line 20. Every other field in the same function is written safely and deliberately: heading.textContent at line 30, and the field() helper at lines 7-13 uses textContent for both the label and the value. So the file demonstrates the safe pattern three times and departs from it once, for the one field that is long-form and user-authored. The body is written by the client with no sanitisation anywhere in the path: createNote passes it straight through (notes.js:31-40) and updateNote spreads whatever patch it is given (notes.js:45-48). No DOMPurify or equivalent appears in the tree.
findings.impact: Script stored in a note body executes in the browser of anyone opening the share view - and the comment at share.js:15-17 says who that is: the site contact a supervisor sends the link to, plus any signed-in user who views the note. Execution in that origin carries the viewer's Firebase session, so the payload can act as them through the Firestore SDK, which given F-39 and F-40 means reading and rewriting their org's notes and profile. With F-40, any org member can plant the payload in someone else's note.
findings.recommendation: Use textContent, or sanitise with an allowlist library immediately before assignment if the rich-text field must render markup. Sanitising at write time is not sufficient here because a second writer (updateNote) reaches the same field.

triage.reason: No sanitiser sits between the read and the sink: the value goes from getDoc (line 20) to note.body (line 26) to innerHTML (line 39) in the same function, and no sanitising dependency is present in functions/package.json or referenced in web/src.
body is authored by a client through createNote/updateNote (notes.js:33 and :45) with no server-side validation; the comment at share.js:18 describes it as the app's rich-text field.
innerHTML parses its argument as HTML; that is the distinction the same file draws by using textContent everywhere else.
No Content-Security-Policy is set anywhere - firebase.json's headers block (lines 10-15) sets Cache-Control on JS and CSS only - so nothing reduces the impact of execution.

scope.established_by: The client-sink enumeration over the tree returned one innerHTML assignment and no dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html or document.write. The safe siblings in the same file were then read to establish that the departure is local to this line.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows it. The function is the share view's renderer and runs for every note it displays.

findings.title: Every signed-in user can read every inspector's profile across all organisations
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: any signed-in user reads all profiles
findings.evidence: firestore.rules:30 is `allow read: if signedIn()`, and signedIn() (lines 6-8) tests only that request.auth is non-null. The collection is not scoped by org in the rule or in the document path. What the documents contain is established by the writer: auth.js:24-30 stores displayName, email, role, orgs and createdAt for each user. Registration is open self-service (auth.js:35-39), so obtaining a session that satisfies signedIn() requires no invitation.
findings.impact: Anyone who registers enumerates the platform's full user directory - email addresses, display names, roles and org memberships for every inspector of every customer organisation. The org membership lists are also the input an attacker needs to exploit F-39 productively, since they reveal which org ids exist and who holds admin.
findings.recommendation: Restrict profile reads to the subject and to users who share an org - `allow read: if request.auth.uid == uid || (resource.data.orgs.hasAny(profile().orgs))` - or move the directory behind a function that filters by the caller's org. The comment at line 28 describes a per-inspector record, not a public one.

triage.reason: The documents carry email addresses and names of identified individuals, written at auth.js:25-26; that is personal data under any reading.

Nothing declares the directory public. The comment at firestore.rules:28 describes it as display name, home org and role for each inspector - an internal record - and the neighbouring catalog rule shows what a deliberately public collection looks like in this file (line 24, `if true`).
The condition is authentication alone; no org, membership or ownership predicate narrows which profiles a given caller may read.
Client code reads profiles directly through the SDK (auth.js:19), so the rule is the only control on that path.

scope.established_by: Enumerated the fourteen allow statements and classified each by the condition it applies; this is one of two read rules whose condition is bare authentication (the other is the catalog's `if true`, which is intended and ruled out). The document contents were established from the single writer, auth.js:24-31.
scope.narrowed_by: Registration is required, so this is not anonymous - but createUserWithEmailAndPassword at auth.js:36 is open, which makes the requirement a formality rather than a bound.

findings.title: The note export builds CSV by joining raw fields, so a note title or body breaks out of its column and can carry a spreadsheet formula
findings.unaided_label: fieldnotes: csv fields unescaped
findings.evidence: Line 97 is `return [doc.id, note.ownerId, note.status, note.title, note.body].join(',')` and line 100 prepends a header and joins with newlines. There is no quoting, no doubling of embedded quotes, no newline handling and no neutralising prefix for a leading =, +, - or @. title and body are free text authored by inspectors (notes.js:33-34), so a comma or newline in either shifts every subsequent column, and a body beginning with = is a formula when the file is opened in a spreadsheet. The result is delivered as a download by the client: share.js:45-50 wraps data.csv in a Blob of type text/csv and clicks an anchor.
findings.impact: At minimum, corrupted exports - a note body containing a comma silently misaligns the columns for that row, and one containing a newline splits it into two. At worst, a formula in a note body executes in the spreadsheet of whoever opens the export, which for the common engines means a prompt to run an external command or a data-exfiltration formula. Low because it requires the recipient to open the file in a spreadsheet and accept a prompt.
findings.recommendation: Emit RFC 4180 CSV: wrap every field in double quotes, double any embedded quote, and prefix a field beginning with =, +, - or @ with an apostrophe or a tab. A serialiser rather than a join.

triage.reason: title and body are free-text fields written by clients through createNote/updateNote with no character constraint anywhere in the tree.
The sink is a text/csv document handed to the user as a download (share.js:45-46); spreadsheet applications evaluate leading-operator cells on open, which is the form in which this is dangerous.

Real but bounded: exploitation needs the recipient to open the export in a spreadsheet and, in current versions, to accept a warning prompt; the column-shifting half needs no prompt but is a correctness defect rather than a compromise. Per FP-10 the severity drops to low and the finding stays written down.
The payload's carrier is the note body, and the reader is a member of the org receiving the export - a second principal with data worth reaching.

scope.established_by: Traced the one CSV producer in the tree from its assembly (index.js:95-100) to its consumer (share.js:44-51), and checked each interpolated field against the escaping applied to it - none is applied to any of the five.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing narrows the encoding defect. It is a second, independent defect in a function that already produced F-37, which is why COV-01 mattered here: the missing authorization is the obvious finding in that handler and the encoding is the one underneath it.
